- An open -service in connection with the Men's Ifible lass was held on Sunday afternoon, Mr. T. S. •Steel presiding. Miss Alice Bridge-and Mr. Arthur Griffiths rendered sacred solos, and the "Guardian" band ,con- ducted by Mr. Barnes, played selections. The speaker was the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, vicar of St. Barnabas' Church, who took for his -subject "Prayer." The offertory was in aid of the funds of the Infirmary.

solo Miss E. Lee ; song "Marguerite ", Miss S. Lee, ; duet" Gipsy Countess "Misses E. Lee, :aid H. Bowyer; recitation "The frowning angel"' Miss C. Gamble ; song "-Angels ever bright and fair "Miss A. Littlewood ; -song, " Barney O'Hea " Mrs. Sheath (encored) ; song "Gipsy's warning ", Miss K. Bowyer ; duet "Two little girls in blue Misses E. Thornily and N. Bowyer (encored). Two dialogues were well carried out : "Sarah Lilly's firmness "and "The next door neigh- bours". Mr. J. H. Thornton accompanied. The usual votes of thanks were passed and an enjoyable meeting was closed with the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was an "open meeting" in connection NI ith this society on Sunday, and the church was filled with mem- bers and their wives and lady friends. The timir was occupied by the Rev John Yenge who observed that -there was a good deal of charm connected with the P.S.A. meetings which did not seem to belong to other meetings on Sunday. He had wondered z-hether it was because they were a bit unconventional that,everybody seemed more at home when attending the meetings. The rev, gentleman proceeded te refer to the presences of Mr. Johnson, of the Charter-street Ragged School, Manchester, and alluded to the excellent work which -was being done in connection with that institution. Not only was it a Sunday School but there was also a dispensary and a working girl's home. The com- mittee of the Wycliffe Society were hoping o be able to forward a subscription to the Charter-street school out of the collection.—Mr. Thomas Johnson gave an interesting account of the work carried on in Man- chester and alluded to-some of the good results which had followed. They had acquired a house known as" The Old Victory" the licence for which had been discontinued It was the intention of the Charter-street Ragged School Committee to transform it into a dispensary and hospital under the name of "The New Victory ". He referred to the blessedness of the -work carried on amongst the poorest in Manchester slums and said he had felt the truth of the-promise that they -would be blessed a thousand fold in blessing others.— The Wycliffe choir sang the anthem "God so loved the -world," and also the selection "There is a green hill," the solo part in the last named being efficiently taken by Mrs. R. H. Pearson—The President announced that 15 new members had been enrolled, thus increasing this year's membership to 143.—The service was also taken artin by Mr. A. Downes (assistant hon. secretary) and Mr. William Beswick.

div.head: Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit. • Quarterly Meeting.
div.p: Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit. • Quarterly Meeting.

'There was a large attendance at the quarterly meeting, ,of the Warrington circuit held on Monday in Bewsey- road Church. Prior to the meeting tea was partaken +of. The Rev. G. IL Carnson, who:was heartily congratu- lated on his recovery from sickness, took charge of the meeting. Mr. George Weaver, the senior circuit steward, presented the accounts which showed that a debit balance of £7 155.1 d. had been decreased to £2 Bs.9d The Chairman read the list of members in the various places in the circuit, and the total &owed a member- ship of 827. On the proposition of Mr. George Weaver, seconded by Mr. Withenshawe (junior circuit steward) all the ministers were thanked for their services and invited to remain in the circuit for another year. Many meraberspresent spoke of the great services rendered by the ministers, and the vote was most heartily and unanimously carried. Each minister responded and accepted the invitation to remain.—The circuit stewards -with Dr. Bennett and Mr. Povey, were appointed repre- sentatives to the Synod.—The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees presented the results of the Foreign Missionary meetings throughout the circuit. The total amount receivee was 250 Is. Bd. showing an incrsase of EH on the past year. The Chairman reported that Hatton Chapel had been sold.—The Rev. %V. J. .C. Neville presented the school returns. There are 291 Sunday school officers and teachers, and a 517 children on the roll, the largest Sunday schools being those of Silver-street and Sankey Bridges. The day schools have 1,247 children on the registers with an average attendance of I,o47.—Mr.Moss, referring to the death of Mr. Brown, of Lyrem,spoke of ithehigh appreciation of his long and valued services to the Warrington circuit, which was universally held by local Methodists, and moved that a letter expressing these opinions and condoling with Mrs. Brown upon her sad bereavement be rent. This was•carried unanimeusly, and after the invitation of Penketh friends to hold the June meeting at Penketh had been aocepted, the meet- was closed by the pronouncing of the Benediction. Ebenezer Church, Buttormarket-street.

Anniversary services were held in the above place of I worship on .Sunday. The preacher was Mrs. Lee, of I Liverpool who gave eloquent addresses in the morning and evening. In the morning, the choir gave an ex- ; cellent rendering of "Blessing the children (Prince of • Peace), the solo being well taken by Miss K. Bowyer. Two anthems were effectively rendered in the evening, viz :—"Be near us" (soloists, Miss K. Bowyer, soprano, I and Miss E. Lee, contralto), and "What are these. ' In the afternoon there was a very good congregation when. the choir appeared to very good advantage in the I cantata, "The Ruler's Daughter." The soloists were Miss E. Littlewood (soprano)' Miss E. Lee (contralto) Mr. R. W. Cook (tenor) and Mr. Heseltine (bass). A male gm:tette was rendered by Messrs J. Geary (treble), R. W. Cook (alto), T. Hughes (tenor), and C. J. Sheath (bass), and a duet was given by Mrs. Dutton : and Mr. Beseltine. Mr. .L H. Thornton officiated as . organist and choirrcaster and Mr. A. Cook gave the con-. nective readings. An orchestral band ably carried out their duties.—On Monday evening the ladies gave the ; annual tea and concert when there was a good attend- 1 ance. The platform had been lit up with fairy lamps and presented a very pleasing appearance. The follow- ing programme was well rendered by the ladies:— ' choruses "Come lassies and lads " 'White Sails " "Chinese umbrella" and "Home sweet home "recita- tion," Owd Dan's fiddle ", Miss L. Sheath; pianoforte

div.head: BRIGHTEST BRIGHTEST LIGHT IN THE WORLD.
div.p: THE BRIGHTEST BRIGHTEST LIGHT IN THE WORLD.

A London Electrician exhibited the other day'a new form of arc lamp which gives a light, beside which the most'brilliant electric light ever previously seen looks like a smoky lantern. This extraordinary light is pro- duced by electrifying the vapours of Mercury. Without the aid of a particle of Mercury a still Brighter Light has, by Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people, been brought into, thousands of homes. All over the country they have restored the light of health to tired eyes, the rose-pink of beauty into pale cheeks. Miss Beasley, the landlord's daughter at the Railway Inn, Oldbury, Birmingham, said these pills, three years ago, brought light into her life which she feared had gone for ever. 'I was in such a terrible state," said she, "through that ever' prevalent malady, ana3mia, that I could not even dress my hair. I was just like death: people turned round to look at me. I used to fall down fainting in the road. I could not digest food—in fact, I had no appetite for it. Dr. Williams' pink pills quite cured me, and I have remained well, eating freely and working with ease. Undoubtedly these pills saved my life."

Local Spiritualism. - Anniversary services were held in the, Spiritualist Hag, Belisey-street, on Sunday, to celebrate the organization of the Society six years ago: Mr. Coun- cillor J. T. Ward, of .Blackburn, spoke encouraging wordsito the Lyceum and adult visiting members in the afternoon, and a very interesting meeting was the result. In the evening Mr. Ward again occupied the platform, giving a practical address on social ques- tions, Mrs. Newton, who, when residing at Stockport was a frequent visitor to the society, had come from Southport to renew her acquaintance with 7lie friends, and kindly gave several clairvoyant delineations at the public meeting and the after circle. On Monday evening a public tea was held, when a good number of friends sat down to a capital spread, the edibles having been given by various members. After tea the President (Mt. Stout) briefly reviewed the work of the society during the past six years. Mrs. Newton followed with words of cheer and encouragement to further effort. Miss Furness sang "The *dear home songs," with taste and feeling, and Mr. Kearns gave a recitation entitled " Wait a week or two," and for an encore sang a humorous song. After a few re- marks by Mr. Pemberton and Mr. Foster, the meet- ing developed into a social, the remainder , of the evening being pleasantly spent in games and dancing.

div.head: ONCE TRIED The Examiner, Friday, March 20, 1903. ALWAYS USED.
div.p: ONCE TRIED The Examiner, Friday, March 20, 1903. ALWAYS USED.

head with eau de Cologne, and Mrs. Bedowen had the company of Inspector Tait all to herself. She was quite composed, having done all that could be done under the circumstances. No blame could attach to her in any way.

"Well, Mrs. Bedowen," said Tait, who was a dry, lean man with cold blue eyes, "and what do you know of this matter?" "Nothing, sir; absolutely nothing." "Ah! Then tell us what you do know. It is all nonsense talking of .absolutely nothing. You must know something." "I don't* know who killed my master," saki Mrs. Bedowen, "and I don't know at what time he was killed. No doubt Dr. Pascoe, who has just gone up, may be able to tell when my poor master died." "When did you see him last?"
_ "About ten o'clock. He came in at that time from a card party at Colonel Gillard's, and sent us all to bect"
"What do you mean? How did he send you to bed?"
"Well," said Mrs. Bedowen, coolly, "it is no our :usual time I admit. We usually retire at half-past ten o'clock. But Aer. Tremewan said we were to go to bed at once, and we were all in bed by ten."'
"Are you talking of yourself and your fellow', servants?"

"I am talking of all of us, sir. Mrs. Tremewaix and Migs Tremewan went to bed also." "Did Mr. Tremewan go?" "I don't know; I was in my bed. When retired at ten he was still downstairs." "Did he express his intention of sitting up?" "No.. He. said nothing. He was not the man to say anything." "Humph! I should think not," murmured Tait, who knew what kind of a bully Francis Tremewan was. "Did you hear any noise during the night?" "No: Not a sound. I came down this merit- ing at seven as usual, and entered this room to see if the housemaid was cleaning it. Of course she was not, being in the kitchen gossiping with the cook. I saw "—Mrs. Bedowen swept the roam with an expressive gesture.
- "You saw what I saw," said Tait dryly; "and the window was open?". "Wide open. The shutters had not been closed."

"Were they not closed as usual last night?" "I can't say. It is not my place to look after them; Emma is supposed to close them. As Mr. Tremewan was out, I think it likely she closed the window and the shutters. She could hardly have left both open, fool as she is. If she had I should have known." "From whom—the_ girl herself?" _

"Not her," said Mr- s. Bedowen grimly, "she would never open her mouth. No, Mr. Tremevian would have raised a storm last night had he found the window opened. He was always very par- titular about it being closed at night." "Most people are," said Tait after a pause, "and yet, humph! Tremewan was a man likely to make enemies."
"I should think it highly probable," replied Mrs. Bedowen, coldly, "but he was a good master to me, sir, and don't like speaking ill of the dead."

"You don't understand," said Tait, looking at her keenly, "I wish to know if Mr. Tremewazi was exceptionally particular in having his shutters up. If so it might prove that he had some enemy, and expected an attack from such an enemy." "Who no doubt came and murdered laim," mid Mrs. Bedowen scoffingly. "Well, sir, I "really -rmenot help you there. Mr. Tremewan was al- ways very particular in having the shutters closed, but so was Mrs. Tremewan, and so is everyone so far as I know. This is a lonely house, and there are some valuable things in it. I always saw that the house was shut up when I went to bed. lam afraid of burglars.' "nut youi did not lock up the house last night?' "Only the back part," admitted Mrs. Bedowen. Mr. Tremewa,n hustled me to bed, and -mid he would look after the rest of the house himself."

"The front part of the house?" "Yes," replied the. housekeeper, who was be- ginning to be restive under this minute examina- tion. "The drawing-room and the dinipg-room, and of course the study: I know nothing about the locking up of these. "Has anything been stolen?" asked the Inspec- tor, after a pause. "Not that I know of. But, of course, I have not made any particular examination, Mr. In- spector. The idea of robbery didn't enter my head." "It has entered mine, however. Just take Jordan with you—he's one of the constables— and go round the house. Report to me if any- thing is missing. .It may be robbery." Mrs. Bedowen shook her .head and pursed up her lips. "I'm sure I hope so," she said omin- ously ; 'but it looks like revenge to me." The Inspector turned suddenly and faced her. "What makes you say that?" he asked. "Do you know anything?" "No," replied the housekeeper, doggedly, "I 'don't. It was your talk of the thutters being up that pat the idea into my head. But now you mention it, I will nay that Mr. Tremewan had plenty of enemies. I believe there was hardly a man had a good word to say for him-or woman either for the matter of that:

"Humph," said Tait, stroking his chin; "is that all you can say?" "That is all," replied Mrs. l3eclowen meeting his inquiring' look in the most open manner. "And what next, sir.?" "Send the other .ervants to me." Mrs. Redowen vanished, and in due time the other servants came to be examined by the In- spector. Emma said that she had closed the window of the study and had put up the shutters at the usual time.

"And when Might that be?" asked Tait. "Six o'clock in winter." said Emma; "and I did put thorn Up. Mr. Treinewan was so par- ticulac about Nixing the study locked up. He said he would dismiss me if I ever neglected to nee to it." _ _ _
"Was the door ever locked?" "La no,. sir. I'm talking of the window and these flutters."
"You are sure you closed them at six?"

"I could take -Bible oath on it, sir." You'll have to take it at the in- quest," said Tait with a dry staile. "Well, that's all right. Did you hear any noise?" "No, sir. Me and cook sleep in the same room at, the back of the house. We never heard any- thing, sir." Do what he might Tait was unable to discover any evidence likely to throw light on the mystery of Tremewan's death. The servants all swore that they had heard no noise, and also that they had been perfectly ignorant of the tragedy until it was announced by Mrs. Bedowen the next morning. There remained Mrs. Tremewan and her daughter to examine. As the widow was still unable t 45 speak, Inspector Tait asked Dora to come down to the study. - She appeared-,even paler than usual, but answered his questions with all candour. At the same time she was careful not to say too much. She wanted time to con- sider her evidence. _ .

"Do you know if your father expected a visitor last night, Miss Tremewan?" "I can't say," she replied, after some hesita- tion; "be certainly sent us to bed, but he did not say if he intended to wait up to see nyone." "Did you hear any noise during the night?" Dora hesitated. "Well, I did," she admitted. Inspector Tait brightened. Here was his oft- asked question bringing an answer after all. "And what did you hear?" Thereupon Dora explained how she had heard someone at the door of her bedroom and how the had risen to find that it was fastened. She also detailed the discovcry of the rope • by Mrs.. Bedowen. Tait listened to all this very atten- tively, and then went uptairs to see the rope for himself. It was still there. "What do you make of this?" he asked.

Dora • shook her head with a despondent look. I don't know what to make of it,' she replied. "I could not understand why I .hould be locked in.y, "Why did you not make a noise?" Well, Mr. Tait, the fact is I thought that my father Lad locked me in." - -
" Why should he do that? Were you on bad terms with him?"

"Oh, dear, no. We got on very well together. But I think myfather had a visitor lltst night, and was afraid lest I might interrupt the interview. For•that reaFon he faAened the door quietly." / "-Have you any idel, who the visitor might be?"
_ "No. I did not know he explted anyone. That is only my thoury "

"We may yet find a reason," was the significant reply. "But if Mr. Will was in the house, your father—as I understand you to say—might have fastened you in so that you might not interrupt." "My father knew that if Mr. Will came I tiould certainly not interrupt. He would mg; fasten me in for that reason."

"Then I can conjecture no other. And mind you, Miss Tremewan, it is your own suggestion that you were fastened in on that account." "No. I never said that," panted Dora, grow- ing more and more confused. Tait squared his shoulders and leaned forward. 'See here, Miss Tremewan," he said delibe- rately, "I have no right to repeat gossip, but in this instance I think lam justified. It is known that your father disapproved of young Mr. Hanna- ford. In fact, I have reason to believe that your father ordered him out of this house. At all events, Mr. Will and Mr. Tremewan were on the worst possible terms." _ _
"Ana for that reason Will would not come here on a secret visit."

" Ahl That is what I want to get at. As yet —save for the ,strange fact that you were fastened in—l do not know if he did come; But .for. no other reason would your father have taken such a precaution with regard to you. If Mr. Will did come, I am sure that the interview was a stormy one, and —" Dora rose with a flushed face and a heaving bosom. "Do you mean to imply that Mr. Hanna- ford murdered my father?" _"I imply nothing. I want to get at the facts." "You are theorising " retorted Dora. "I am sure Mr. Will is in London, and has been there all the time. I don't believe he was here. If he had intended to come I should have known." "And you did not know?"

"Certainly not. As a matter of fact his father insisted that he should not return to Dart- bridge." "Ha!" cried Tait, .rubbing his hands. "Then fhat supplies the reason for a secret visit. Mr. Will knew that his father would be angry if he knew of his return. He therefore came at night, when he thought Mr. Ha.nnaiord would not hear of his visit. I am more certain than ever, Miss Tremewan, that your assumption is the right one."
"My assumption r What_ do you mean?"
"Why. That you were fastened in your room to prevent your. interrupting a stormy interview between Mr. Will and your father."
"I assmne nothing Of the sort," cried -Dora, indignantly. "You: are putting words into my mouth."

"Well, well. It is natural that you should be indignant. But if you do not wish to answer any more questions I can see Mr. Will. He may reply—if he dares to." "Dares to. You are making a case up against him without reason."
"We'll see about that. At all events the only way to get to the bottom of this matter is to interview him.. Can you give me his address, Miss Tremewa.n?" and the Inspector took out his notebook.

•" No," replied Dora sharply and promptly. "If you want that you must see Mr. Hannaford, senior. He is the right person to apply to." "Quito so," answered Tait, soothingly. "I will see the father. But lam quite sure, Miss Tre- mewan, that you know that address." "If I .do I refuse to give it to you," she re- tailed.

The Inspector tapped his teeth with his pencil, and looked at her agitated face gravely. "You are going the worst. way to work to defend Mr. Will," he said, after a pause. He stands in no need of defence," she replied haughtily, and rose. "If you have quite done with me, Mr. Tait, I should Eke to go." "Certainly." Tait rose also, and opened the door with great politeness. "I have done with you, Miss Tremewan, for the—present" His .significant look dwelt in her memory as she went up to her room. By her foolish blurt- ing out of Will's name she had involved him in trouble. ,This stupid officer fancied that he had here a clue, and would follow it up in bus blunder- ing way. She could not believe that Will had been in the house. And yet in her own mind she could not. account otherwise for her being fastened in. Certainly if Will had come at all he would have come secretly, both because his father lisui forbidden him to return to Dartbridge and bemuse he was seeing his father's enemy.. But why should he come at all? What could his errand be? Dora's head ached with perplexity. She could find no answer to these questions. Will had not been in the house. She was certain of that. He had not killed her father. The very thought was madness. If she could only learn who was the culprit. Was there no clue Suddenly she thought of the handkerchief which the pug had been tearing in the study, and which she had put in her pocket. No doubt it belonged to her father. She had no reason to think other- wise. But in the faint hope triat it might reveal something she took it out and looked at the initials. They were "W.G.H.," and Were worked in red silk. Dora grew pale when she saw them, and dropped the handkerchief with a cry. "Will's," she murmured, with white lips. "William George Ha,nnaford—his initials—his handkerchief. Ho was in the study after all." She paused, then dropped on her knees. "I have destroyed him,' she, sebbcd, "I have destroye4 him 1"
But why should he lock you At r" "I really can't say. You know as much as I 'do. "

The Inspector looked puzzled. He could not .anderstand what relations could exist between a father and daughter that would impel the former to lock up the latter. Still, it was a common report that the late Tremewan was extremely eccentric. As this ,thought crossed his mind, Tait began to wonder if in this known eccentricity might be found any clue to the •motive of the crime. He hardly knew what question to put next, and therefore asked the first, and most natural, that came into his head. "Was there anyone in the house at that time whom your father did not wish you to see?" Dora looked nervous. This was a leading ques- tion, and she did not very well know what to say. Had her head been clearer she would have bad some idea of what course to take. But the catastrophe of the murder, and the persistent examination of this Man confused her mind. She evaded a direct reply, and tried to collect her wits.
"Am I bound to answer you?" she asked, 'trying to appear calm. • "I think it will be as well:"

"In that case," replied Dora, rushing on to destruction. "I must admit that my father did. not wish me to see Mr. Will Hannaford. There were reasons—certain private-7her voice died away,. and she flushed. The Inspector whistled. He had heard the rumours of the strife between the house of Tre- mewan and Hannaford. His w,ife had informed him, for Mrs. Tait was the greatest gossip in the neighbourhood, and the Inspector encouraged her prymg propensities. Many a time had her chatter helped him in his professional work. It seemed that her scandal about the loves of Will and Dora might .contribute some nedessary evi- dence towards the solution of this mystery. After some thought Tait asked a blunt question. "You think that your father's visitor was Mr. Will Hannaford?" - "No," replied Dora quickly, "that is impossi- ble. He is in Louden.' "-He might have come down from London to. see your father —" "There was no reason that he should have come secretly," interrupted Dora. "or have come at to lute an liour-'

div.head: AFTERWARDS.
div.p: AFTERWARDS.

For a moment or two Dora stared at the house- keeper in silence, hardly able to take in the full meaning of her words. Then she recollected the light in the study so late at night, the man who had entered the house, and finally the fact of her door being fastened. At length she found her tongue. .
"'Who murdered .In'm ?" she demanded, leaping out of bed.

"I don't know," replied Mrs. -Bedowen, sitting down on a chair near the floor. "Lord bless me,. Miss, don't look at me in that awful way. I went to the study as usual to see that the housemaid was looking after the cleaning of it, and I found your father sitting at his desk." "Dead?" asked. Dora in a low voice.

"Strangled," replied Mrs. Bedowen with a nod. "But who did it I know no more than you do. Come and see Miss. We must tell the police." "The police," stammered Dora, hurriedly put- ting on her clothes—the first that came to hand. f` Must we httve the police." "Of course," replied Mrs: Bedowen, im- patiently, "and a fine scandal there will be over this matter. There hasn't been a murder in Dartbridge for years and years. And to think that your poor father should be the one. Oh, dear! oh, dear!" and the great fat woman wrung her hands in a paroxysm of grief. _ _
My mother, Mrs. Bedowe'n, does she know?" Mrs. Bedowen shook her head. "I haven't had the heart to tell her."

"She must know at once, then," cried Dora, 'hurrying to the door, "but in the first place"— here she broke off. Her eves fell on a thick piece of rope which was tied to the handle of her door. It lay half across the passage, and one end of it was immediately under the handle of the opposite door. "What does this mean?" she asked, pointing 'it out to Mrs. Bedowen, and the woman again shook her head. She seemed bewildered.

"I was going to ask you that, Miss," she said helplessly. "I came up to tell you about this dreadful thing, and I found that rope tied to the two handles. It was tied so tightly that neither door wculd open. To be sure there is no one in that room, but your door Miss;---did you know. that *wouldn't open?" Dora nodded, and tried to arrive at some con. 'elusion. "I knew last night," said she faintly, but I did not understand. I was going to ask • this morning who had done it." . ~"r wonder who did?" mused Mrs. Bedowen, with her eryes on the rope. "It was tied RO tightly that it took me quite a time getting it loose. ' I was almost on the point of getting 4 knife. But Lord, Miss!" she went on in a quavering voice, "here we are talking and your ; poor father is lying dead below under his own roof-tree."

"I'll go. Mrs. Bedowen you go up to my, mother's room and bring her down." Mrs. Bedowen apparently did not like the mis.; sion, for she hung back. But Dora had no time to argue. She ran down the stairs quickly, and entered the study. Mrs. Bedowen had closed the door, and when Dora opened it she saw her father seated as the housekeeper had described.. He was in a chair before the desk, and leaning back. His head hung on one side, and round the neck was a thin silken cord. The first glance told Dora that the cord had been taken from one of the window curtains. She mechanically looked and saw that while the Curtain to the left of the window was looped up the other hung straight. Without doubt the assassin had snatched the cord from the right curtain and had flung it round the neck of the unfortunate man. He could have struggled very little, for everything - was, quite in order. The shutters were fastened back, and the one window looking out towards the road was wide open. After a pause Dora touched the dead man's hand. It was cold. There was no doubt that Francis Tremewan was a corpse. "The man who crossed the stream of light," muttered' Dora; " who was it?—why did he kill my father? Where " She broke off at the sound of growling, and looked down .to see the Japanese pug worrying a handkerchief. He had followed her into the room, and had dragged the handkerchief from under the table. Hardly thinking what she was doing Dora picked up the handkerchief. She never thought of looking at it, thinking it belonged to her father, and as she heard the sound of a wild voice coming nearer she thrust it into her pocket. At the. same moment her mother, still in her nightgown, rushed into the room.

"Francis! Francis!" .cried the poor woman,. staggering towards the corpse. "I want youl Francis. They Fa y you are dead. I do not"— here she touched the waxen face, and the chill contact told her the truth. With a shrill cry she recoiled. "Francis! You are—dead. Dora. He is dead. He is murdered—he is—is—oh God—oh!" She fell forward in a faint, at the very feet of the husband who had loved her so well.

Dora bent, down to raitte Mrs. Tremewan's head. At the door was Mr. Bedowen. and over her shoulder stared the other servants, white- faced and with scared expressions. "Help me to take her to her room," said Dora, trying to gather her wits togetheis. "Quick, some of you."
"-Cook, Emma, you help Miss Tremewan," cried Mrs. Bedowen. "As for me, Miss, I go for the police."

"One inoment." said Dora, as the housekeeper was about to retire, "was the window open when you entered the study this morning?" "You see the room, Miss, .exactly as I saw. it," said Mrs. Bedowen in a. low voice, and with a shudder. "I have not. touched a thing." The girl nodded, and assisted the other ser- vants to carry her mother upstairs. The house- keeper hastily put on her hat, and Dora, looking' from the window of her mother's roam, saw her going down the highroad into Dartbridge. She had gone to fetch the Tolice, and it was, when this thought flashed across her mind, that Dora for the first. time began to grasp the idea that this was not a simple death, but a terrible and cruel murder. "But who could have done it?" she wondered while attending to her mother. "Who was the man? Shall I tell the police what I saw?" She debated this .point for a time, and' then resolved to hold her tcfngue,until the inquest took place. There would be time enough then to relate what she had seen. The rest of the day was like a bad dream to the girl. Mrs. Tremewan recovered only to fall into another swoon as she remebered 'liter loss. The police inspector, with three constables, took possession of the home, and the general public eongregated outside. Several reporters made their appearance, but the inspector—he was an old Army mane-would not let them come in. He knew well enough that murderers often escape by means of the information they get from the papers, and .Inspector Tait was resolved to keep all his information. to himself for the present. After- wards the reporters could make. public what they liked. This reticence on his part did not .make him any the more beloved by the members of the fourth estate. But as Tait always enforced his rule the reporters had to abide by it. Dora was kept .so Much beside her mother dure ing that awful day that the task of looking after the police devolved on Mrs. , Bedowen. That woman rose to the occasion, and recovering her faculties, somewhat scattered as was natural by the catastrophe, attended to all matters con- nected with the presence of the authorities in a" wonderfully composed ...manner. This behaviour was all the more praiseworthy, as she was won- dering in her own mind whether Captain Max had strangled the master. As yet she could not decide, but she had her suspicions, and deter- mined to find out if she could. In the meani time she attended Inspector Tait in the study. The corpse had been removed after the In 4 spector had seen it sitting at the desk. It wag now laid out in the bedroom of the late Mr. Tre4 mewan' and a policeman was on guard at the door. Dora was with her mother hathine her

div.p: THE GREAT EASTERN'S DECAPOD.

The most wonderful locomotive ever designed, ,and at the same time the one that promises to be .the most efficient, has just been completed at .the Great Eastern Sheds at Stratford, and named the Decapod. The Great Eastern Railway Company have for some time past been hesi- tating, in common with many other big lines, as to whether steam or electricity must ultimately 'become the universal power. The many draw- backs attending electrification have been the means of the Great Eastern Company devoting their attention to the greater possibilities of steam. Mr. Holden, the well-known locomotive designer, had in mind an engine that would practically equal the electric motor in power and quick attainment of speed. The directors requested him to design such a locomotive, and not only has this been done: the engine has been constructed and has run its trial trip to such satisfaction that it has been decided to adopt it generally. It has been made to carry heavy suburban traffic, and possesses the double qualification of speed and power. It can haul the heaviest suburban train put on the line, and attain a speed of 30 miles per hour, 30 seconds after putting on steam. The Decapod is a pon- derous thing to look upon. Its boiler is of such, dimensions that there is no room for any funnel worth speaking of. The engine, in fact, looks all boiler. There are ten wheels, all coupled, which is more than the heaviest goods engine •ever possessed before. These wheels are much smaller than the usual driving-wheel, but are, nevertheless, capable of attaining a great speed.

THE NEW LONDON THEATRE.

presents from the Emperor Menelik of Abyssinia, with whom he is very popular. Herr Seeth is a Swede by birth, being a native of Holstein, and has always been closely identified with wild animal training. Lions are his peculiar hobby. His beasts he calls his "boys," and as his "boys" they are thoroughly in hand. He rarely punishes them, considering such a course worse than unwise. To transport his lions from the Continent to England costs him something like Zcoo, while he values the whole of his show property at no less a sum, than £30,000. His first appearance in England was met with success such as no entertainer of this type has ever been been favoured with, and this, the second and last time when he performs before London, is sure to beat in popularity even the record established by his first visit.

Sir Charles Wyndharn made such a financial success with the theatre bearing his own name that he decided to build a second next door to it, and last week he opened it under the name of the New Theatre before a brilliant audience. The architecture is of the "free classic" order, and it has a- frontage of seventy-six .feet to St. Martin's Lane. Inside it is beautifully decorated and very comfortable. As announced, Sir Charles Wyndham gave the whole of the proceeds of the opening night to the Widows and Orphans' Fund, which, together with many voluntary subscriptions, amounted to a large sum. The piece selected for the, inauguration of this new play-house was. "Rosemary," the charming .-"t'

div.head: LONDON AND GLOBE CASE.
div.p: LONDON AND GLOBE CASE.

The arrest of Mr. Whitaker Wright in America, whither he had absconded under an assumed name, has given general satisfaction, as it was feared that the police had a long stern chase in front of them. His arrest, however, simplifies matters considerably, and there seem § little fear that there will be any serious trouble • in extraditing hint: Last week, when by Mr. Justice Buckley's order a summons was is- sued against him, \ it was found that he had left the country and gone no one knew where, and this early Cap- ture was the last thing in the world that was antici- pated. Tales were flying about of yacht journeys to Egypt and many other, moves, and the police declared that they had no clue. Now that the case is sub judice 11,0 comment is 'permissable upon Mr. Whitaker right's actions ; but it is allowable to say that rerYone will be glad to have the whole of the .'-°ndon and Globe business thrashed out to the very bottom, as there has been so much talk and scandal about it. The position of the -Attorney-General, after his refusal to prosecute, has been very much discussed in the face of Mr. Justice Buckley's decision, and, even more so, his promise to amend the law to meet such a case has come in for strong criticism, as from the judge's decision it seems that, if Mr. Whitaker Wright is guilty of the crimes imputed to him, there is ample law to cover the case. In connec- tion with this unsavoury piece of finance great names have been most unjustifiably bandied about, and one good effect of the trial will be to put a stop to this reprehensible gossip. In the city the liveliest satisfaction is expressed at the prospect of the whole affair being brought before a court of justice.

div.head: HERR :ULIUS SEETH'S RETURN.
div.p: HERR :ULIUS SEETH'S RETURN.

Herr Julius Seeth who some three years ago, created quite a sensation in London with his Performance at the Hippodrome in a cage with twenty-one forest-bred lions, is now appearing again at the same popular place of amusement, and exciting even more interest than on his first visit. It will not, however, be able to run for very long, as the theatre has been leased to Mr. 'Forbes Robertson, who within a month takes possession with "The Light that Failed," which has, it seems, settled down for a good run. Sir Charles Wyndham, of course, appeared in person to open his new theatre .and afterwards made, one of those little speeches for which he is sci. famous. THE LATE DEAN BRADLEY.

The death of Dean Bradley cannot be said to have been in any way unexpected, as he had been ill for some weeks and gradually sinking-. For many months :he had, without being dangerously ill, been very feeble; and owing to his great age it was _known that he could not last very long. TJp to last August he continued to held DOS] t i(j11 Orr West-
the position of
Dean
minster, and was
a well - known
figure in the Ab-
bey, to which he
was devoted. From his position
many herieditary
rites fell to his lot at the Coro- nation of King Edward but on account of his
feebleness, though
retaining office, he preferred to de- pute them, fearing suck a breakdown as actually oc- THE LATE DEAN BRADLEY. curred in the case

of Archbishop Temple, who has gone before him. It was announced directly after the ceremony that Dr. Bradley had formally resigned his office, obviously only having retained it for the sake of the Coronation. His successor, however, was not nominated. until October, when Dr. Armitage Robinson succeeded him. Apart from his episcopal career, Dr. Bradley was a great scholar and a noted schoolmaster. Under him Marlborough came very much to the front, and the late Lord Tennyson once remarked to a friend: "I did not send my son to Marl- borough, but to Bradley." The late dean is a familiar name to all schoolboys, and his re- written edition of Arnold's "Latin Prose Corn- positiOn" is the standard work on the-subject. From Marlborough he succeeded to the Master- ship of University College, Oxford, and left a great mark behind him upon his appointment to the Deanery of Westminster. Dr. Bradley has died full of years and honour,, and will long be remembered with affection and r(sp2ct by those who came into contact witit him. Dr. Bradley published a .series of Westminster Abbey lectures • on Ecclesiastes, and a. similar series on the Book of Job in 1887. Soon after Dean Stanley's death he was invited by the Philosophical Institution of Edinburgh to deliver a course of lectures on Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, which were afterwards published. His last years were 'spent in the quiet of the Abbey cloisters, and he had no greater satisfaction than to conduct parties of visitors round the sacred shrine, and point out the historical monuments, and describe the beauties of the ceurch he loved so well. Almost his last public function was to assist in the Coronation of His Majesty Ring Edward VII. It is pathetic to remember that of the great ecclesiastical personages who took a prominent part in that historic scene six months ago two have already departed to other spheres. Doubtless it was' with a pang of grief that he felt himself compelled to withdraw from the Office he had so ably filled. He was -very Successful as a' master. Among others who emphatically testified to this was Dr. Temple, who went to Rugby as Headmaster not a very great time before the retirement of Dr. Cotton from Marlborough College created a vacancy, which Mr. Bradley was ambitious to fill. "I know very few men," wrote Dr. Temple in reply to the young master's request for a testimonial, "who are equal to you in the com- bined power of teaching and governing. The care, the kindness, and the firmness with which you manage your house, the life and energy with which yon carry on the work of your form, the clearness and precision of your teaching, the hold which you obtain over the affections and respect of your pupils, are all to marked not to have already impressed my mind with a very. high ntiroate of your value hersa

div.p: The Examiner, Friday, March 20, 1903.
BILE BEANS AND INDIGESTION=

Mr. JohnMeggatt, a miner of Drongan (Ayr), suffered from indigestion for eight years. 'Pain after every meal, sleeplessness, and gradually decreasing strength were the symptoms. His blood became impoverished, and when he sustained a cut or bruise in the course of his work, it festered and was bad for a long time. -He underwent a course of Bile Beans and in a few weeks was not like the same man. ! Now, he says, he is in the best of health, can enjoy hearty meals, and "is in fine condition." When he gets acut or bruise—as miners so often do—it no longer festers, but ,heals rapidly and gives no trouble, showing clearly thathis blood is now in the condition it should be. Bile Beans, purely veget- able in composition, are nature's remedy for all liver and digestive disorders. They don't merely alleviate ; they cure !

THE LEAGIJE.---FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

The return match between Warrington and Broughton Rangers was played on Saturday at Wilderspool in cold and showery weather. There was a crowd of quite 5,000, nevertheless, and notwithstanding the heavy ground a good game was witnessed. \Carrington had Isherwood absent, and the Rangers.were short of Hogg. Mr. E. H. Smirk, of Wigan, was referee, and the teams were as follows :

Warrington: Hallam' full back ; Fish, Hockenhall, Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Edmunds and Duckworth, half backs; Boardman, Morrison,Jolley, For3ter, Edmondson, F. Swift, W. Swift, and Naylor, forwards. _

Broughton Rangers.—Fielding, back; Winskill, Wil- son,_ Barrett, and Kirkham, three-quarter backs ; S. James and W. James, half backs; Orion, Ruddick, Woodhead, Preston, Scott, Beetham, Thompson and Whitehead, forwards. Wilson beat Fish in the toss, and decided to play with the wind. Swift kicked off for Warrington and a strong forwArd dribble at once gave the Rangers' defenders a lot of trouble, Fielding and Wilson being somewhat lucky in stopping the rush. Warrington still continued to attack, and Edmunds and Harris almost broka through: A free kick to Broughton enabled them to reach the opposite side of the field, and Wilson receiv- ing a pass from James was floored a yard from the line. This put Warrington on their metal, and Fish intercept- ing a pass got clear away, but in passing Fielding, the latter was lucky enough to pause him to stumble, andhe fell when he had no one else to pass. The rain now came down, though to the discomfort ,especially of the defenders. A free kick was given to Warrington, which was, however well rerilied to by Fielding; and the Rangers attacked hotly. The onslaught ended with Barrett sending dead with a flying kick. For some timeafter the drop out play continued at centre until passing by Duckworth, Dickenson and Harris took the ball tethe quarter flap, andEdmunds taking up the run- ning was floored under the goal post. Exciting play followed, and Wilson floored Fish close to the goal line. Things now looked well for Warrington natil Hockenhall mulled badly, and Wilson and W. James kicked into safer quartere. The latter players played a combined dribble, and almost got over. This put the Rangers in a very geod position, and a series of scrim- mages took place under the goal post, from one of which Winskill received the ball, and dashed over, W. James failing at goal. After the restart Warrington pressed fora time but powerful kicks put the Rangers but the defensive, time, nothing further was scored. Half- time: Broughton Rangers 3points, Warrington nil. Omm restarted, and Morrison made his mark. Field- ing reptied well to Fish's kick, and the opening move- ments were at centre. Fielding, however, mulled so badly that Harris floored him near the goal line. The forwards got Broughton out of the fix, and good runs by W. James and Wilson put them in, a much better position. For a time play was very' scrappy, but at length Fish got a chance, and, was not stopped till close to the line. Much amusement was caused by the crude efforts of both sets of forwards, to form scrimmages, and a tremendous amount of, time was lost in conse- qitence. A free kick, fell to Warrington, and Fish failed at goal. After a host of chances a score came very unexpectedly to Warrington. Dickenson dribbled through the Broughton. team almost half the length of the field and scorefi a try all on his own. Fish failed at goal. Wilsonnearly broke through after this reverse but Harris tackled well. Fish likewise got away, and Fielding brought off a fine tackle. Full time arrived with Warrington still attacking. Final—Warrington 3 . points, Broughton Rangers 3 points.

div.head: RUNCORN v. LEIGH..
div.p: RUNCORN v. LEIGH..

The above match was played on Saturday at Irwell Lane.—Leigh played a representative team. For Rim- corn Jolly took the place of Houghton, Walker taking Jolly's. position at half. The ground was heavy, a strong end to end breeze blowing. Runcorn lost the toss, Richardson forcing the visitors to defend. A penalty sent the ball backand Richardson set his line in motion, Moran failing to hold. Jolly,with tricky play,made up the deficiency but a dangerous forward dribble carried the leather back to the Runcorn quarters. After uninteresting play Moran got away only to slip with a clear field in front of him. A couple of. minutes later Richardson tricked his man and handed to Jones who slipped over at the top corner, Farmer failing at goal. Runcorn were forced to defend after this, Jolly, Walker, and Pride keeping the visitors out in gallant fashiOri: Bennett, however, marked in front of the sticks from a low catch and Molyneux dropped a splendid goal. Leigh continued to press add for a time it looked as though they would score 'again but Jones 'worked the danger away. After this the Linnets rushed to the other end where Richardson and Jolly had two unsuc- cessful drops at goal. Eventually Price sheered through his opponents and grounded over the line, Farmer fail- ing at goal. Half-time Runcorn.two tries, Leigh, one goal. The change of ends saw Runcorn assume the aggres- sive Pearson being called upon to save. From the scrum Molyneux tried a short kick, Price intercepting and racing up the field, Walker, who was following,scored between the posts. Farmer added the necessary points. Gaudy and Bennett nearly got over, Richardson clearing. Pearson again brought off a splendid save grassing Moran. Play eventually settled at midfield where the visitors repeatedly got possession, a front rank move- ment being stopped by Price. Runcorn maintained the upper hand to the last. Final :—Runcorn, one goal. three tries (eleven points) ; Leigh, a eoal (two points).

div.head: WIGAN v. WIDNES.
div.p: WIGAN v. WIDNES.

These teams opposed each other at Wigan, More 5,000 spectators. The visitors ha strong wind in their favour during the initial half, and monopolised the attack, Hughes scoring a couple of smart trios, which enabled Widnes to change ends with a lead of six points to nil.

In the second half the visitors offered a splendid -defence, whilst their forwards proved a superior 'set to the Wigan front rank. Anderson, Dickinson, and Duffy each endeavoured to cross only to be smartly tackled, and the home representatlVes failed to get • through. Result tries (6 points), Wigan nil, 'reams:— Wigan—Mason;-back; Dickinson Wilcock, Threlfall, and A. Duffy, three-quarter backs; 'Nelson (captain) and Anderson. half backs; Ball, Hilton, Conj.:4r, Halliwell, Ellison, Beesley, Hatton and Topping, forwards. Widnes—J. H. Tilley' luck; T. Peacock, J. Taylor, G. Bown (captain), and J. Hughes, three-quarter backs ; A. Taylor and J. Lally, half backs; G. Aspey. J. Levshon, T. Lynch. M. McDonald, W. Rigby, H. Riley, J. Power, and M. Webster, forwards. Referee. Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton Range: s. Touch judges, Messrs. T. Little, St. Helena, and F. Turner, Warrington

div.head: ST. HELENS v. HULL
div.p: ST. HELENS v. HULL

, 1 ' Played at St. Helens. Hull played with the wind,and the home forwards made a splendid drib ble, Lut got off- side, and a moment later Wade kicked to the other end, , after which Parry' made 4 good run, but passed forwa rd. 1 Barnes ran well and passed to Liversage, who scored a 1 grand try for St. Helens, Lee failing at goal. Briers next got over for St, Helens, and Lee again failed. The visitors worked their way into the home half, and Cook i mule a good effort, but his endeavour to find an open- ing for his wing failed. Hull again worked to the home iline, and Parry picking up scored a good try, Taylor

failing at goal. Half-time score ;—St. Helens 2 tries, Hull 1 try. On resuming Taylor, Goddard, and Morgan made a brilliant run, and the last named looked all over a scorer when Banks ran across the fleldand tackled him in splendid fashion. Hall dropped a goal for St. Helens Parry sent the ball across to .Lewis, who, took it splen- didly, and scored under the posts, Goddard kicking a goal. St. Helens worked up again, and Carney dropped a goal, giving St. Helens the lead again. Result :—St. Helens 2 goals, 2 tries (10 point's), Hull 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points). BRIGHOUSE RANGERS v. SALFORD v. SWINTON.

Played at Weaste, before 14,000 people. Preston started for Swinton against the wind, and Salford quickly pressed, Gnl liths dropping a goal after ten minutes' play. Saon afterwards Lomas getting posses- sion near the corner, dodged over near the posts. The same player landed a goal. Swintou were badly beaten forward, and there was no stopping the Reds. Swinton did a little better, but were neverreally dangerous. On the other hand, Salford made several dangerous rushes, but Williamson relieved the pressure by kicks into touch' while Chorley prevented liarter from scoring, but a few minutes from time he dashed over and gave Salford another try, Messer's place-kick failing. Re suit :—Salford 2 goals 2 tries (10 points), Swinton nil.

div.head: SALFORD v. BATLEY
div.p: SALFORD v. BATLEY

Owing to these clubs being engaged in the cup ties earlier In the month, the return League match was post- poned, and was played on Monday on the Salford ground. Salford placed in the field the same team which defeated Swinton, but Batley were without Goodall, Auty, and Phillips. From start to finish Salford proved themselves far superior to the visitors, and such a weak defence was opposed to them that scor- ing was camparatively easy. In the first five minutes Bell had crossed the Batley line, and despite the fine efforts of Roebuck, Davies, and Fitzgerald the score rose so rapidly that when half-time arrived Salford had the large lead of fourteen points to nothing. Batley played up a little better in the second half, and through Haigh and Burnett they managed to score eight paints. Salford, however, were never really tested, and they added another fourteen points to their half-time score. Result :—Salford, two goals and eight tries (28 points); Batley, one goal and two tries (eight points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. OLDHAM
div.p: RUNCORN v. OLDHAM

The abAve teams met at Irwall-lane on Wednesday afternoon. The ground had not reaovered from the heavy rains of the previous day and there was a vary high wind blowing from end to end.. A good cro<d of supporters travelled with the Oldham contingent and there masa good attendance. Both clubs played repre- sentative teams.

Runcorn won the toss, commencing operations with a I strong wind behind them. Neat kicking placed Runcorn on the defensive, Jolley with a fine kick finding touch with the . visitors' 25. The attack was repulsed but a neat bit of work by Jolly and Jones nearly passed the top corner. A moment later Richardson marked in front of the goal, Farmer's kick dropping outside. Moran further improved matters the same players later beating the men and contesting the game on the Oldham line. The defence was stubborn a kick at Houghton giving the visitors achance to avert danger. Civil next got away along touch, Jones and Houghton stopping his career. Shortly after Moran was deservedly applauded for neat play. Exchanges left the advantage with Runcorn, Jones placing the visitors on the defensive. A Moment later from the scrum Jolly handed to Richardson who sheered through his opponents in magnificent style and scored one of the best tries of the season. Farmer easily added the major points. The ball had hardly been set in motion when Civil and Rees got away along touch, Houghton and Jones sav- ing in the nick oetime. After a little uninteresting play Price gathered from a high kiok and kicking well up the field Richardson secured, Thomas mulling, and popped over at the corner. Farmer failed at goal'. Just before the interval Jones got away, after beating his man, and kicked across the field where Moran dropped between the posts. The referee disallowed the point on the ground of alleged offside play. Half-time: Ruacorn one goal two tries, Oldham, nil. The restart opened out with a sensational run by Walker and Moran. A moment later Richardson and Jones got over but the ball rolled dead. The visitors after this, made a furious onslaught on the home line Jolly saving. The ball, however, was speedily sent back, an anxious time ensuing. Moran wortced the leather away but the attack was continued with force, Houghton being forced to kick dead. The visitors con- tinned to find touch and pegged away at the bottom corner Farmer at length clearing. A beautiful round of passing between Richardson Price, Moran and Hes- keth further improved the home position. Both sides pressed in turn, a fine kick by Price enabling Runcora to assume the. aggressive. The ball was speedily sent to mid-field, where M 3ran intercepted a pass and raced up .the field. with both teams following behind. He easily beat Huzzey and slipped over at the corner flag. Farmer failed at goal. Tue game had hardly been re-opened When Moran again got away in the same manner, bat the ball was ruledback. Final :—llatacorn, one goal, three tries ; Oldham, nil.

div.head: Wycliffe Temperance Committee Social.
div.p: Wycliffe Temperance Committee Social.

The Wycliffe- Temperance Committee brought a successful season to a close by a social gatherin, which was held in the Memorial Buildings on WeS- uesday evening. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. B. Farrar, who delivered an interesting speech, in which he contrasted what he termed the world's programme with that of Christ's. The programme of the world of to-day seemed to be "Keep your mouth shut ; go with the stream and mind your own busi- ness.'' Christ's injunction to His disciples, he said, was just the reverse. What, he asked, would have been the position of the temperance movement if everyone had followed the world's programme ? The)* would have been no progress to record, and there would never have been such an Act of Parliament as the recent Licensing Act. The progress of temperance was largely due to men who had not 'kept their mouths shut. In con- clusion, Mr. Farrar congratulated the Wycliff.: Tem- perance Society upon the work of the past session, which he believed was the most successful since he had known Wycliffe.—Mr. Joseph - Owen also ad- dressed the meeting and observed that the Wycliffe Temperance Committee were co-operating with other organizations in the town for the inculcating of tem- perance, principles.. They had also a band of .hope society and were represented on the Warrington and District Band of Hope Union and also the Lancashire and Cheshire organization. He thought they at Wycliffe were doing their fair share of temperance propaganda work. (Hear, hear.) He proceeded to refer to the death of Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., whom he regarded as one of the finest Men who had ever. stood on the Temperance platform. A musical programme was submitted, including pianoforte solos by Miss Smith and .Miss B. Wells, recitations by Mr. Whitfield and an .auto-harp solo by Master Whitfield. Miss Griffiths was the accompanist. Parlour games were afterwards indulged in, Mr. F. Morrell acting as M.C. Refreshments were handed round during the evening.

div.head: "OLD BLUES' " PRESENT TO MR. AND MRS. EDWARD ROSE.
div.p: "OLD BLUES' " PRESENT TO MR. AND MRS. EDWARD ROSE.
Twenty-ona Years as Master and Matron of the Blue Coat School.

It must be very gratifying to Mr. and Mrs. Edward I Rose, after twenty-one yesrs of devoted service in the capacities of Waster and matron of the Warrington Blue Coat School, t,n know that they have earned the grati- tude and high esteem of the pupils who have passed through their hands. If evidence of these cordial feel- ings of appreciation and good-will were needed, it was forthcoming on Tuesday evening, when the institution was the scene of a happy gathering arranged for the purpose of celebrating Mr. Rose's birthday, and at the same time presenting Hr. and Mrs. Rose with some tan- gible recognition on the part of the "Old Blues" of their recent completion of twenty one years' service in the I positions which they have so admiralily occupied. The j gift took the form of a solid silver tea and coffee ser- vice and a silver mounted tray Which bore the following inscription :—" Warrington Blue Coat School, 1882- 1903. Presented to Mr. and Mrs. Ed. Rose by former pupils of the institution as a mark of affection and esteem upon their completing 21 years as master and matron.' Present as well as past scholars participated I in Tuesday evening's function and parents and friends of the children attended. An excellent tea was served in one of the large rooms, and it goes without, saying that this part of the proceedings passed off in the happiest style. The event of the evening took place in the chapel, which had been brightly decorated with flags and streamers. Councillor Forshaw occupied the chair and the scholars were seated on the platform. The children took a very lively interest in the event, and punctuated the various speeches with vigorous applause At the outset the chairman said he was sure they all wished Mr. Rose many happy returns of the day. He was pleased to preside over that gathering of" Old Blues "and friends because they were met to do honour to whom honour was due (Hear,hear)—to commemorate the 21st year of the connection with the school of Mr. and Mrs. Rose, and to give them a small token of their appreciation of their valuable services. (Applause.) Mr. and Mrs. Rose were the right people in the right place— (cheers)—and the trustees did a very good and a very wise thing when they appointed them. They were worthy of the positions they held. During the time they had been entrusted with the management of thelaititution they had extended the usefelnesS of the iffstitution very much, new lavatories, dormitories, schoolrooms, dining- rooms, and baths having been added, and the number of foundation.scholars had increased from 40 to 70. These feats showed that Mr. and Mrs. Rose had done an excellent and useful work. They were proud to see Mr. and Mrs. Rose looking so well, and hoped they would lone be spared to continue their good wOrk. (Applause.) An enjoyable concert was then proceeded with, the opening items being a chorus by the children. Mrs. Short very sweetly rendered " Kilarney" and a recita- tion by Miss L. Matthews was well received. Mrs. Adamson and the Misses Allen, E. Carlisle and F. Car- lisle gave an instrumental quartette "Sur Lis Floto " ,in an able manner. Mr. A. Grounds was as entertaining as ever in his humorous sketch" Sloshem Coronation festivities," which provoked great hilarity. Mr. R. Caomyroe then made the presentation. He said that those who were pupils at the school 21 years ago would remember the bad state the school was in. After Dr. Bowes died they had for four7months a really rough and naughty time. He enjoyed it for one, but it came to a close. If it had gone on the probability was that many of those who were present that night would not be occupying their present posi- tions. (Hear, hear.) After referring to the great interest which the children took in the appoint- ment of the new master and matron the speaker said that to occupy such positions as those held by Mr. and Mrs. Rose was no sinecure. It was a task that required aieat tact as well as considerable ability, as they had not only to act as ordinary teachers, but as parents to several hundred children. "Old Blues" had a great deal to'be proud of when they remembered the great strides which the -school had made during the past twenty-one years.. Although the sinews of war were I provided in the shape ,of funds it was the actual ad- I ministration of those funds which had the good effect; it was the wise administration of the money that had been the cause of the progress of the school. (Applause.) Mr. CRONIPTON spoke of the great improvement for the comfort of the children which had taken place at the school during Mr. and Mrs. Rose's period of office. It would be impossible for the old pupils present that night to adequately express their gratitude to the master and matron. 'He asked Mr. and Rose to accept their small present in the feeling with which it was tendered. I (Applause). Mr. H. Bennett then effectively rendered a song. Mr. ROSE had a very cordial reception on rising to reply. He said he hardly knew in what words to express his very sincere and heartfelt thanks for the kind things which had been said about his wife and himself and he Naas afraid he Would find it still more difficult to express his feelings in regard to the handsome present. It was very gratifying to feel and to be assured that in endea- vouring to do their duty they had been so fortunate as to gain the goodwill, esteem and affection of many of the pupils who had passed through their hands. From the "Old Blues," who were at the school previous to his conling he led always received the greatest kindness and the hearty welcome they gave him when he first came to Warrington was still fresh in his memory. Many friendships were formed at that time which had con- tinued uninterruptedly to the present time, and he - trusted they would continue as long as they lived. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Now they found another generation of "Old Blues," some of whom ware in the school when he first came to it, while thera were others who had been admitted and passed through it during the past 21 years who were anxious to show their ap- preciation of the efforts of his wife and himself for their welfare by making them such a handsome peesent. He supposed the feeling was natural. He (the speaker) had the greatest regard and respect for his old school- master, who was still living, but when to the position of schoolmaster was also added the responsibility of a parent he was not surprised that the feeling should be intensified ; indeed he shonld be very grieved if he thought that any of the pupils who had passed through his hands had not at some time or ether given a thought to them, considering the positioa Mrs. Rose and him- self had occupied towards them, and the interest they took in their welfare when they were in the school. It was that kindly feeling which showed itself among their old pupils from time to time which encouraged Mrs. Rose and himself and supported them at times, when otherwise they would have been discouraged. (Hear, hear, and applause). There were causes for discourage- ment as well as for congratulation, but he felt when he looked round and saw so . many of the old pupils occupying good positions, and filling them with such credit to themselves and to the institu- tion which gave them their start in life that they bad great cause for thankfulness. (Applause.) Reference had been made to the improvements which had been carried out during the past 21 years to try to bring up the school to the highest possible state of efficiency, not only with regard to the instruction given but with reference to the domestic arrangements, and he couldassure all present with regard to the alterations and changes which had been male that he had always receifed the hearty support of the trustees, to whom he was very grateful. He had been inn good many institu- tiohs—he never missed an opportunity of visiting them When he was in other towns—but he considered that theirs would compare very fav,ourably with the majority with respect to the arrangements which had been made for the comfort, convenience, happiness and well-being of those who were fortunate enough to be elected to participate in the benefits. (Applause.) He thaught all the "Old Blues" would testify to the anxious care and motherly kindness with which their little ailments had been attended to, and to the still more anxious care which had been devoted to pupils who had suffered from illnesses which appeared likely to develop seriously. In again thanking the old pupils for their present, the speaker said that Mrs. Rose and himself would set store by it as one of their choicest treasures, which would remind theni of the esteem in which they were held by their late pupils, and cheer them when they might feel a little downcast. They would treasure it all their lives and he was sure it would be prized by their children when they had passed away. (Applause.) He would express the fervent hope that 'God's blessing might rest upon ell "old Blues" and that they might have comfort and happiness in this life and attain still greater happiness hereafter. (Applause.) Cheers were then given for Mrs. Rose_, and after an in- terval the concert was resumed. Another instrumental quartette " Fidaro " was rendered and Mrs. Short and Afr. Bennett gave songs,Master R.,Essenhigh recited and an excellent ventriloquial sketch was submitted by Mr. Grounds.
The accompaniments were played by Mrs. Massey and Mr. F. Rose.
The following gentlemen constituted the presenta- tion Committee 'Messrs. F. Short (treasurer), W. Rutter -(secretary), Rowe, Lowe, Crank, Bromley, Crompton and R. Hughes.

KILLED BY ELECTRICITY. An inquest was held on Tuesday at Mansfield on Reginald William Seale, fitter at the Sherwood Colliery, who was killed on Saturday afternoon. It appeared that the deceased and another man were shot-firing by electricity at the top of the shaft. After a shot had been •fired deceased stepped, towards the wires apparently with the object of discon- necting them. He was seen to fall, and died almost immediately. The jury found that decbased was killed accidental contact with a" live" wire, and recom- mended that the special rules governing the shot-firing at the colliery be strictly enforced.
