div.p: A conspicuous figure has THE LATE MR. passed away from the Par- CAINE, M.P. liamentary life of our time. Mr. W. S. CAINE, M.P. for the Camborne Division of Cornwall, died on Tues- day from heart failure at the home which he had chosen because it was within easy distance of the royal palace of Westminster. Though Mr. CAINE'S Parliamentary experience dates back no further than to 1880, it has coincided with many striking events; and Mr. CAINR hi/11961f was a singularly complete epitome of the period over which his lifeas a member of Parliament extended. He was one of those men • who are not afraid of being confronted with their past when it appears to be inconsistent with their present. He was a massive, solid, serene looking man, who appeared to. be liable to few changes of temperament. But, like Sir GEORGE TREIISLYAN, a man of very different physique, he voted against the first Home Rule Bill, and a few years later accepted Home Rule and fought gallantly under Mr. GLADSTONE'. The truth was that Mr. CAINE was a most scrupulous man, and his change of conviction on Home Rule was really an outcome of his conscientiousness. He was not a man who held his opinions lightly; they were deep-rooted in his nature. Though a man of. massive build, he had a delicate and refined nature, with a nervous sense of the importance of diving actively and usefully, and with the clear blue, soft, candid eyes of the man who is in earnest without being in haste. Mr CAINE was devoted to two great causes, tem- perance and India. His interest over the affairs of our Eastern dependency was so eager, his study of everything which related thereto was so close, and his watchfulness in Parliament was so relent- less, that, as occurred also in the case of Mr. BEADLAUCH, he was known as" the member for India." A pathetic light is thrown on this faithful- ness to the interests of the Indian subjects of the Crown by the fact that at the time of his death there was on the Parliamentary papers a question which he had put down in relation to the recent Durbar. He was not a persistent questioner, nor was he a frequent speaker in the House of Com- mons; but he was always an effective member, commanding respect and consideration, and be- ing recognised as a man whose motive power was to be found in his own genuine convictions. He had many up 3 and downs. in his Parlia- mentary life, hut the less fortunate incidents of his career were as honourable to him as were his experiences of political good fortune. He followed the banner of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN for a while ; but when he saw into what kind of political company that was leading him he resigned his seat in order that he might resume his former position of allegiance to the Liberal party. It never struck him—as it has strucksome others in recent years that he might retain his seat whilst discarding the views by virtue of which he had obtained it. Mr. CAINE was a manly man all throu4h,with a certaie careless joviality which led a distinguished politi- cian to speak of him in a humorous moment a 8

" that genial ruffian." There was a large, calm ' strenuousness about him. The cause of temper- ance had in him a supporter such as it can ill afford to spare. He was vigilant and determined. Under his unexcitable exterior there was a con- stant watchfulness. Without fuss and withou hurry, he was always doing services to the man good works with which he was identified. His nature was such that none of those who differed from him regarded him with other than friendly feelings. He will be greatly missed in the Hous - he will be sincerely mourned in the country; no where more sincerely than by the electors in the Camborne Division, whose interests were so near to his heart. He was a man of great probity, of iofty ideals, of real public usefulness, and of un- blemished character.
There are some points of RYE ELECTION.— view fvom which the Liberal MR. BALFOUR AND victory in the Rye division "THE TRADE." is more remarkable even

- _ than Woolwich. The turn- over of Conservative votes has been greater for one thing, and the election is therefore to a large extent indicative of a popular reaction against the • present Government. In most instances in which) *during the last few years, the Liberal party has won seats from the Conservatives, victory has not depended on a diminution of the Tory vote, but en a rally on behalf of Liberalism. The Tory %Party went on polling up to its former strength, smnetimes a little more, sometimes a little less,was beaten by the new voters or by the votes of elec- tors who had previously abstained. It is now made convincingly clear that this condition of things, and the state of publie feeling of which it was the expression, has passed away. The Govern- 'Merit is being deserted by its supporters—and not 'merely in great industrial constituencies like Wool- wich, but in wide-spreading rural parliamentary divisions like Rye, and, as we hope shortly to be able to say, 4ike Chertsey. Such an event as the Rye election, following on the, phenomenal victory Of Mr. WILL CROOKS, fully justifies the now al- most generally prevalent feeling: that if there Were to be a general election the Conservative Party in the House of Commons would practically be swept away. The effect produced on Mr. BAL- -POUR, by the news from Rye was very remarkable. On Tuesday he received a deputation from the G.-Jciety of Friends, which made some suggestions SS to the restrictions of ',betting. The PRIME MINISTER was curt and scarcely civil. He bowed the deputation out with the assurance that its memorial shall receive the careful consideration of 'himself and his colleagues. Mr. BALFOUR'S demeanour was strikingly different on:Wednesday When he received a deputation from the Beer and Wine Trades National Defence Leagne. He was then all charm and affability of manner. There was 12.0 talk of the merelyclistomary kind about " care- Int 'consideration." There had been considera- tion beforehand—very careful consideration, we Should say, of the urgent necessity of stopping at this stage the incipient, but increasing, revolt "the trade". The PRIME MINISTER threw him- 'Self into the armsof the deputation without reserve. Be made a strong, even a vehement, speech against the magistrates who have been reducing the " mber of licenses, and practically appealed to ,quart sessions to reverse the decisions at Tb• the licensing magistrates ,have arrived. ts la Conduct exceedingly characteristic of Mr. "'• a. He is as full as LORD GEORGE HA.MIL.• -ON' or the idea that" we must do something for our friends." He has on no occasion that we can call to mind risen to the conception that states- manship should be concerned only with the affairs of the community at large. His mind is full of the idea that if a Government is to make itself safe is must gain the goodwill of the various Powerful " interests ." ; that it must not regard the mere elector, but only those bodies or those Individuals by whom the electorate is believed to swayed. The moral. he appears to have drawn Lrom recent events is that the Government is sup- eed—quite unjustly, of course—to have injured " Public-house interest, and that this impression •1111.'et be removed at all costs. The Church, he Z,rns to have reflected, has steered the vessel con- the Governmeht and its fortunes on to b seodbank, and "the trade" must now e e to Mployed in the cvacity of tug-boat drag the endangered vessel back into saf sive Waters. This is a cynical view of statesman- and its necessities, no doubt, but it is just a view as Mr. BALFOUR might be expected to 1:1". He is like the PHARAOH who hardened his t °art On an occasion on which he had no reason congratulate himself. Warnings such as the tholvvich and Rye elections estrange him more and more from the great body of the people, and confirm him in the impression that the Ministry can only serve itself by binding the classes and "ue " interests " more firmly to the Governmental ear. The advice which he gave in regard to the lilt-leaner sessions on Wednesday is very ligely to ;343 taken. Courts of Quarter Sessions are almost variably very considerate in regard to licenses nat have been taken away. On every corn- Misiion of the peace, there are large numbers of magistrates who have ceased to act except on Widely separated occasions. These may be expected, under the spur of Mr. BALFOUR'S ex- hortation, to swarm on to the bench when licensing appeals are to be considered. They will no doubt M many, if not in most, cases imdp what the licensing justices have dpne. The men who 'habitually neglect their duties as magistrates will oast their votes against those who have given *their most careful consideration to the matters emning up for review on an occasion when they are almost certain to be out-voted. This is what .elt. BALFOUR asks for. It is a shockine. and Ztartling appeal for a PRIME MINISTER to make, .blit it may be that now the much shaken and edres.Tgled Government has again attached to ''Self the wavering support" of the trade."

Tha members of the Warrington Society were, last Thursday evening,privileged to hear and learn .!'")niething about the Garden City movement, tihrough the medium of Miss Illingworth, a Brad- -4"lrd lady, whose eloquence and personal charm on platform could not have been exceeded. Lady '‘An.turnr% are, as a rule, noticeably competent, but lIS Illingworth must surely sand in a class by ,2"Elf —at any rate those people who heard her the old Academy were decidedly of that opinion. Irgt, and foremost she is obviously an enthusiast 'l') the subject she has taken lin. and if her efforts t tr)."commend garden cities fail then we are cer- ,'?'nlv an unregenerate race. To many people the 1,-rardon City Association is hut a name—a pleasant ieninding title—and nothing'more. In reality it anidealistic and earnest organisation which makeq •ght. of the difficulties in the way of materialis- ,,;-lz its Utopian scheme. There is even good cause vr). believe that the first Garden City will, at no J. „!? distant Joe, become an established fact. "e hope so! Garden cities present an admirable

solution of the over-crowding and housing problems Were they to become general, the existence of the masses would very nearly approach life in Utopia itself, but unfortunately it is t-, much to hope that any very extensive adaptation of the Association's ideas will take place in our time. Still, if we get one Garden City it will present an object lesson on the way life in large towns should be lived that cannot fail to have far-reaching effect. There will be no slums in the Garden City,and everything will be arranged so as to give the greatest possible benefit to all in the way of health, convenience and pleasure. At present, Port Sunlight, and Bourneville, :come nearer to Garden City ideas than anything else in I existence, but even they fall very far short of the conception of the ideal city. They are not cities to begin with, and in this fact lies the greatest drawback to their being held up as examples of what the Garden City Association aims at. Never- theless they do away with slums, and encourage existence amid artistic as well as hygienic environ- ments, which is a great advance. With the Garden City oi the future will dawn a new and brighter era in "life here het° " and we heartily wish the Association success in its unselfish, humanitarian scdeme.

The Transvaal War Relief Committee, which did so much for the relief of the wives and children of local reservists and volunteers during the South African war, brought its labours in Warrington to a close last week. The people of Warrington and district generously responded to the com- mittee's appeal for help and the fact that the magnificent sum of £7,259 18s 2d. was raised locally for the relief fund, will be a standing testimony to the townspeople's generosity. The workpeople especially, contributed handsomely to the fund, the contributions from the local works forming a large portion of the total sum collected. It is interesting to learn that there is a balance in hand amounting to £1,386 55., which has enabled the Committee to form a widow and orphans' fund. This will be sufficient to provide an annuity for the maintenance of all the local widows and orphans caused by the war for a period of about 38 years. Such a result is highly gratify- ing, and the annuity will be a source of comfort and help to those who have lost the breadwinner of the household in South Africa. Too often the chief sufferers from the war are obliged to seek parish relief or drift into the Workhouse. The people of Warrington, howevtr, have the satisfac- tion of knowing that they have done something to prevent this undesirable state of affairs by show- ing practical sympathy for the widows and Orphans of reservists.

he annual Me-mbers' meeting was held on Monday last under the presidency of ,Mrs. Harry Baker. The yearly election of officers and committee took place, and addresses were given by Mrs. Baker end Mrs. Eyre. The Secretary's report 'showed an increase of 13 mem- bers during the year. At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. G. L. Davies (in the chair) and Mr. E. unison, Mary Hughes, Gilbert-street, was charged withhaving stolen a pair of boots, valued at 2s. (id., from the shop of Samuel Dodd, pawnbroker, Princess-street, on the 10th Inst. The evidence showed that the prisoner went to Mr. Samuel Dodd to transact some business and after- wards went to Mr. Lightfoot's, Pawnbroker. She offered to pledge a pair of new boots and the manager's suspicions being aroused he detained the boots and sent for the police. Prisoner admitted the theft and was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days in default. •

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[By A CORRESPONDEN].] -'litticv of my readers will regret to learn that the St. Paul's Wesleyan Church; Runcorn, has had to be closed owing to the dangerous condition of the roof. Late last year, it was found that some of the stonework had crambled away and an examination revealed that the greater portion of it would have to be reaewed. After the tenders had been set it was found,on Mr. Wilding making the investigation, that the roof Avit.s in a highl ydangerous condition, some of the rafters literally " halving by a thread." Mr., Potts, architect, of Manchester, subse- quently visited the edifice, and on his report it was deemed necessary to remove and re-construct the ceiling and the roof. The unfortunate part is that the ceiling —which is one of the finest in the country—will, pre- sumably, have to be completely re-cast. The church was built in 18117, being the gift of the late Mr. Thomas Hazelhurst. The services in all probability will be held during the process of renovation, either in Brunswick School or the Drill Hall.

The amalgamation scheme of the Urban Council to include Halton and Weston is exciting some little in- terest in influential matters. Needless to say Halton and Weston are almost bitterly opposed to the scheme. Hopes run high, however, in Urban circles, that the in- corporation will, ere lon,z, be an accomplished fact. Both sides can make out good cases for and against the proposals' fought when the issue comes to be ught out either by the county authority 014 the higher authority, the proceedings should be fraught with interest.

It is pleasing to note that their is little danger of the policemen's social ever again falling through. On Wednesday there was a more jubilant body of the "gentleman in blue" than there has been for twelve months. Thanks to the exertions of Messrs Wood,Cooke and Coventry, the policemen with their wives and sweet- hearts thoroughly enjoyed themselves. It is regrettable that there was a deficit on the last year's social, and should this berepeated I would suggest that the leading tradesmen of the town be requested to contribute. I am sure all "peace-loving, law-abiding " tradesfolk would be glad to contribute their mite to the enjoyment of the stalwart protectors of their hearths and homes.

div.p: FOOTII.ILL.

Leigh journeyed to Runcorn on Saturday and though they were not clever enough to cover themselves with glory they were successful in covering themselves with mud. Showers of 'rain had made the ground inn very heavy state and a trong end to end breeze did not improve the conditions for good foothill. Though the home team lost the toss they pressed keenly in the first half. Both the tries—by Jones and Price—were the result of good .combination. Leigh were thoroughly outclassed and though they attacked

div.p: The Examiner Friday, March 20, 1903.

strongly on several occasions once or twice only I could they be said to be at all dangerous. In the latter half the visiting forwards got possession repeatedly but the backs did not make the use of the chances which they might have done. Jolly, in fact, had but little work to do and really seemed anxious, several times, to join in the melee which he generally initiates. Walker shaped very well at half back. Occasionally he made a mistake in neglecting to part with the leather, but generally speaking, he played a good game. Price, as usual, played a magnificent game, and, with Richardson had a hand in all the passing movements. Butterworth and Jones did their work well, the former play- ing a solid game with few chances to dis- tinguish himself. The brilliant but erratic Moran payed a passable game. If he would only pull himself together :tad put half the spirit into his work as a Price, a Butterworth or a Richardson there would be few wings to beat him. Farmer failed twice to steer the ball over the crossbar but the kicks were from ex- ceedingly awkward angles. On the whole the home forwards did not show up to advantage. If they packed better in the scrums the "Linnets" would be the most formidable opponents in the Northern Union.

On Wednesday at Irwell Lane a grand game was wit nessed between Runcorn and Oldham. The form of the home team was simply superb, the attack and the defence being of the high order one naturally expects from two such exponents of the Northern Union Code. Oldham was beaten all round. Price and Richardson played a wonderful game. The latter scored his first try in a beautiful manner. With a long swerving run he fairly glided past his opponents and was over the line before players or spectators could realise that the effort had been suocessful. It was unquestionably the finest try so far, of the season. Jones was also in rare form, his attack and defence being all that could be desired. Moran gave another exposition of his brilliant tactics. On three occasions he got away with both teams trott- ing behind, and his try was the result of a splendid sprint. Jolly and Houghton, as usual, played superbly and contributed materially to the success of the home team.

div.p: NEWTON D3CTOR'S ACTION. Alother Step in the County Curt Proceedings.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday the ad- journed action in which Drs. John Webb Watkins, and Harold Ernest Watkins, Newton, took proceedings against Gustave Fairall, Eagle Hotel, Ladbroke Grove, London W., the executor of Miry Ann Gorse deceased who up to the time of her death, was the licencee of the Oak Tree Hotel, Newton, either to obtain payment (4423 16s. being the amount of plain- tiffs' account against Mary Ann Gorse for medicine and medical attendance, or failing that, an order to have the estate of Mary Ann Gorse administered, •came up for hearing. Mr. E. A. White represented the plaintiffs, and Mr. H. J. Longton defended. The case was before the Court in December last and was adjourned in order that the Renistrarcould take an account of the personal estate, debts and funeral ex- penses, to make inquiry whether Mrs, Toft took pos- session of theassets as alleged by the plaintiff : 'also to make inquiry whether the defendant improperly carried on the trade, and to certify the result to the Court before March 19th.

it was stated that since the last hearing Dr.- John Webb Watkins had unfortunately died, but his son who acted in partnership with him was present in Court. The Registrar having presented his report to. the Judge, Mr. White desired to call his Honour's attention to certain facts which appeared in the Registrar's notes, and asked his Honour to form a different conclusion from that which had been formed by ,the Registrar. in 'regard to the value of the house- hold goods and fixtures fixed by the Registrar hecontended that it was insufficient:4 The Registrar should have based the report upon the value of the goods at the time of Mrs. Gorse's death and not at the time of the auction sale at the hotel. There as only one document which might have been put in tv ide tic e— the auctioners' sale account—and although the Registrar ruled that Mr. Longton was bound to produce it, Mr. Longton declined to put it in. He -submitted that this was contempt of Court. He also submitted that there was value in the goodwilLas there had been evidence that the executor at once handed ,over the business to Mrs. Toft who was still in possession and that there were upwards,of 10(1 people who wanted the. licence. There was also a bowling green of which he(Mr White) contended there was a delusory sale by auction.. The green was knocked down to a brewery company without the sale being advertised, for the nominal sum of one shilling. His Honour made notes of the objections .and adjourned the hearing until April 23rd when the matters will be fully gone into, and Mr. Longton will reply to Mr. White's contentions. •

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. Bj " ovaiist."

Warrington did not quite succeed in defeating Broughton Rangers on Saturday, but they did the next best thing by making a draw of the =telt. The result is, of dour_ e, somewhat disappointing, for War- rington spectat , 3 do not like to see the team drop a point on the Wil erspool ground; and especially after they have had the best of the game. ,

The fact is. that Warrington should have had four points out of the Rangers this season, instead of two points as the result of a couple of drawn games. Nothing but rank bad football prevented them winning at Broughton, when the Rangers had only half a team in the field. Though Warrington were without Dickenson and. Fish they should; have won on that occasion. Last Saturday also they had numerous opportunities to win the game, but failed to take advantage of them at the critical moment. lam not saying that they played badly, far from it, but there is none of that snapping up of opportunities Avhich one likes to see. Still, all teams miss chances, Runcorn being perhaps the lightest offenders in this respect. As a rule the Linnets snap up all that is available in the way of opportunities for scoring, and to their keenness and reliability. in this respect they owe much of their success.

It was a great misfortune for Warrington to have Isherwood absent owing to influenza. The hope was general that for once in a way Warrington would be able to place a full team in the field, but fate again willed otherwise and the absence of the captain was severely felt. I can confidently express the opinion that had Isherwood been on, Warrington would have won. Kockenhall is rarely a success at threequarter, and on Saturday he bungled passes at a time when ordinary smartness must have resulted in a score. On behalf of the Rangers it must be admitted that they were also handicapped by the absence, of Hogg, Wilson's regular partner on the wing. Still, I don't think Hogg is so important to the Rangers as Isher- wood to Warrington. If Wilson had been missing, the case would have been quite different—as would the result of the match, undoubtedly.

The Rangers had the advantage of a strong breeze in the first half, but they were not immediately on the offensive. iWarrington we,nt off with a rush,Edmunds and Harris getting very hear the line in the first minute. The. first punt by the RangerS quickly changed the venue, and Warrington were kept busy defending. Once again however, they dr we their opponents back and Edmunds threw a certain try away by sticking to the ball in front of the goal .when Dickenson could have scored easily. The "-little tin" for once made an error of judgment and, . I believe, fancied he was nearer the line than Witi actually the case. A moment later Hockenhall muffed a pass which would have given Fish another "cart," and Broughton at once dashed off to the other end. They had been very lucky to escape. The home side were again hard pressed.,and Fish adopted the unusual expedient—for Warrington—of bringing Forster out to check the Rangers' combination. This is doubtful policy at any time, but on Saturday Fish spoiled his own idea by putting Forster on the right side of the germ* where there was only Barratt and Kirkham. The result was that "the Jimmies " slung the ball across to Wilson's side and Winskill got in at the corner -through Fish concentrating his attention on the opposing skipper. Had Forster been between Fish and flockenhall, the Rangers could never have obtained the try they did. However, they led by 3 points at half-time.

Warrington had every confidence in wiping the arrears off on resumption,but it took some time. Fish would have scored five Ininutes after the restart but the whistle sounded for a reason which was not ap- parent to the crowd. Then, though Warrington attacked persistently they could not get through, the Broughtoii backs kicking .vigorously for touch at every opportunity. At threequarter time, Warrington looked as if they might lose. A score CUM when least ex- pected, of course. Hockerthall missed a pass at centre, and the ball went to the ground. Dickenson dashA up and kicking past Wilson 116 went after the oval like lightning, beating Fielding eaSily for speed, and finally dribbling over the line was as fine an individual try as the Warrington crowd have seen this season. Fish could not manage the goal, nor even a penalty later, and Warrington had to be content to share the points, though they had nuvestionably the best of the .game.

Dickenson played the best' °frame for Warrington and Wilson for the Rangers. Both were very pro- minent, the latter appearing to do nearly all the work for the Rangers. The home halves, Edmunds and Duckworth again played well, and it would be folly to separate them. They were quite equal to .W. and S. James on Saturday. Fish was also in good form, but appeared to have lost smile of his speed': It is a rare thing to se him get away three times and be brought down by the full back. Those three fine tackles were a feather in Fielding's cap; but he displayed excellent football throughout the game, and was better than Hallam. The Warrington. forwards deserve com- mendation for an improved display. . They quite held the Rangers, who however, are no great shakes in this department.

Halifax retained premier position last Sabirday by winning at Batlev with an ease which caused ugly rumours to circulate concerning some of the M mint Pleasant cracks. Salford went over Swinton by de- feating the blues at Weaste, and on Minday they simply swamped Batley by 23 points toB point; on the same ground. Just now the Reds are invincible, and a slip by Halifax might result in the Salfordians annex- ing both cups.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

The monthly meeting of the Latchford A.S. held last Monday was very enthusiastic. All the members p esent were invited to participate in the President's , (Mr. Henry Taylor's) hospitality. The paper on "The ' Natural History of a Fish " by Mr. F. J. Emson was well received. The members of the Howley A.S. at their last meeting decided to support the local amalga- mation of anglers. In connection with the National Trades Exhibition which opens on the 30th of March at Bingley Hall, Birmingham, eleven specimens of "set-up " coarse fish, ,caught by local anglers, will be amongst the specimens exhibited. Mr. P. Knight, the general secretary of the Warrington A.A. will attend the executive meeting of the Provincial Angling Asso- ciation which will be held in Binningham to-day. Some local anglers recorded excellent sport at Llan- gollen during last week end (Friday and Saturday.) Mr. William Hamblett registered one of the best catches which has been noted for some time. 301bs in all was the total ; and the fish were all dace except two, and these roach. All the dace averaged Bto 9 ounces each. The exhibition of the catch caused much admiration, not to say excitement, amongst anglers. From the same district, Mr. F. Boyle re- corded a roach of lib soz 10dr, Mr. W. H. Podmore a dace of 93-Ozs • Mr. William Boyle a trout of lib, 3oz, sdr, and Mr. W. Bate several dace of eight and nin- ounces each. Several other anglers creeled nice samples of trout.

div.head: GILCHIST LECTURE AT EARLESTOWii. Labour an Art in English Life.
div.p: GILCHIST LECTURE AT EARLESTOWii. Labour an Art in English Life.

The last of the series of Gilchrist lectures promoted 1 by the Newton-in-Makertleld Lectures Committee, was i given on Monday eveniag in the Town Ilan, Earles- town, before a large audience. The subject was "Labour and Art in English life illustrated by Greek Art "and I the lecturer was Mr. Chas. Waldstein, Litt., D. Ph. D. L.H.D.

! Lord Newton should have presided,bat he wiradto say ; that he was unavoidably prevented from being present. Mr. W.Collingwood took the chair,and after regretting the absence of Lord Newton, said the series had been a very successful one, and he was sure this last lecture would make a very suitable termination. The short acquaintance he had had with Dr. Waldstein, as host, assured him that he would enable them to attain in some measure an interest in Art which war Much needed in that district to enliven their lives amongst the labour in which they toiled. The lecturer said he had just learned that Earlestown and that audience had quite enough but that there might be a want with regard to the artistic side of life. He wished merely„ that evening, not so much to instruct as to stinudate ; he did not wish to bring before them t a continuous and systematic history of any one period of art, and what he wished to prove was that every labouring man, every man who works, has not only- a ! right and claim to share in the lighter and artistic side ! and enjoyment which springs from it, but he wished to I bring home to them the intimate relation Which these facts have to everyone of us. If he were to ask himself 'what he considered, among all virtues, among all qualities which go to make thesuccessful and contented and happy life, he should single out one point, the pos. , session of the sense of proportion, for he believed that I, most of our petty disappointments, and great miseries in life, may be, inmost cases, attributed to the absence !of that important quality. He meant by this, the sense which enables us to regard everyone -of our individual experiences in the proportion which theyholdand ought, ' to hold to our life, taken as a whole. If our imagina- tion would enable us for the time being to step outside otmelves,and to regard ourselves in proper proportion, that we are units of It vast community, and I , small units of the whole congregation, and the claims ; which we have to our self enjoyonent, compared with the claims which our neighbour has, if we were enabled to exercise that sense of proporition, we should be saved • from immense' disappointment, nay, from many of the ' miseries of our existence, for we 'should then realise after all, that life was a happy-one. If that was so with ; • individual lives it was also so with a whole community. The idle man, whose whole life and existence is directed ; towards pleasure, was very likely to lindermin) the health of his body, the development of his soul.and was 'sure to be the sufferer. He confessed it had been a per- sonal grief to hint, when ho compared our country with those of Germany. France' &c., in the way they were trained in the arts of nlay. He felt saddened. to recog- nise how far above us they were, and when he had seen, , on Bank Holidays in our manufacturing districts, what forms of amusement we fro to go through, and how indifferent our working people were to lind Proper :MUNE?, meat, how unstable they were in that kind Of life to what they were in Germany, Prance Sc., he waseaddened. llt was the duty of those who were responsible for great ; national mcivement. to direct their attention not only to self improvement, but those higher forms of intel- lectual eniovinent. refining enjoyment. Everyone ought to have some abso:bing interest ontsida his working side. if we studied the ancient' Greeks, the period of history to which he had devoted most of his life, the ! one thing we learned front them was that, they were far beyond ins in the side of art and side of play. The • Athenian citizen would have been ashamed if he could not have at Imst appreciated every side of life. tie . then procee4ed to illustrate by means of lime light pictures, the rise and progress of Greek art, from the rudest idol-like images toy gradual stages to greater per- fection in the natural rendering of the human figure..
—At the close a vote of thailks was accorded the lee- timer on the motion of M:. D. Forrester, seconded by Mr. T. Parr.

The Lecturer responded and on his motion a similar conipliment was paid the Chairman. Mr. Coiling Wood said that being the last of thg series of lectures, they would be wanting in courtesy if they parted without passinr, a hearty vote of thanks to the secretary, Mr. Ormatid, and the committee who had worked with him. Mr. Ormand had worked most nobly in this cause from its initiation. From the first lecture which had been given he had worked like a slave almost and had brought the lectures to the very successful stage they had reached. (Applause.)

div.head: "THE COUNTESS OF STAMFORD " AND A RUNCORN BANKRUPT'S ESTATE.
div.p: "THE COUNTESS OF STAMFORD " AND A RUNCORN BANKRUPT'S ESTATE.
Application at Warrington County Court.

A lady who lays claim to the !title of " Countess of Stamford and Warrington" appeared at the Warrington County Court on Thursday to make an - application to : His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. Prior to her marriage with Mr. William Gilroy, of Congleton, the lady wag Agnes St. Mary de Grace, and by her awn individual e:Yorts she is now endeavonr- : ing to reclaim the estates which she contends : rightly belong bo her as the Countess of Stam- ford and Warrington. She has 'already become familiar ; in several Courts by her frequentannairances in support and her claims. She is a short middle aged person of respectable appearance, wearing spectacles. On Thurs- i-day morning she sat at the solicitors table until the time arrived for applications to be made and she then .! entered the witness box. . _

Producing a written dlc tnrut • sha Raid siv.. applied for an order, writ o!' sunmums to reopen the bmkruptev , of the late J, Siddy, music seller, of Runcorn, which ' occurred in 1878, the receiver or trustee being Mr. G. .T. Knight, F.C.A.. accountant, Runco.rn,and to mune' Mr. Knight to produce a schedule and accounts of all assets of the said J. Siddy and further to 'give lip all deeds, (loci-talents and papers relating to the RfmcornandCon- gletoe prowrties. She added that her husband, Mr. William Gilroy wts afflicted and could not act on her behalf nor could he support himself 9r her. She con- tended that they had been brought to complete beggary and next door to starvation. His Honour said he could not make an order without Mr. Knight knowing of the application. If the appli- cant would put herself in order he would listen to it, but notice of motion must first be served on Mr. Knight. The Applicant: By whom? His Honour: By any person who is competent to dolt.

_ The Applicant: Or by myself? His Honour: Perhaps you suspect the learned pro- fession. (Lam:hter.) It would be better for you to instruct a solicitor to take the necessary steps to in- form M. Knight of the apnlication. If you do so then you will he in order a Ld T shall beable to judge whether yonrepplication is one of substance. The Annlicant: At nregent you cannot do anything more. May I ask if this Court has jurisdiction in the matter ? (Laughter.) His Honour: I cannot judge of the case until I know the facts. lam told by the Registru, that Run- corn for bankruptcy purposes is within the purposes of this Court. Therefore it looks as though I have juris- diction. Perhaps I ought to be glad in being able to tell you so.

, The Applicant: Tam sure yon will be glad when you hear all the circumstances. (Laughter). His Honour: You must have an aqiclavit prepared and brought into Court,. Th,! Registrar (fr. Ridgway) : The matter appears to be one of some complication. and it would perhaps be better if it wag prep ired by,a, Solicitor. Ills Honour : Yes. It seA•ns to be complicated not, only by the facts but by lapse of time. Therefore I think you had better avail yourself of legal assistance. The Applicant : Mr. .1. Siddy only died about 31 yenTs ago.
- - His Honour : . I cam only sly you should get legal assistance.
The Applicant: T thank you. She then left the Court, apparently satisfied with the advice given.

div.head: EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT.
The Infirmary Workingmen's Com- mittee S3lC3t a Representative.

Councillor John Roberts presided at the adjourned annual meeting of the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee which was held at the Town Hall Warrington,on Saturday afternoon for the purpose of appointing a representa- tive on the new Education Committee. Amongst others present were :—Councillor Burton (vice-chairman) and

Mr. J. H. J. Hampson (Secretary ot the Infirmary and Dispensary). Four names were submitted to the meet- ing, namely, those of Mr. George Walker (Cheshire Lines Engineering Department), Mr. Joseph Taylor (secretary of the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee), and Mr. A. Birch an". Mr. \V. Nightingale, the two latter representing one the forge department and the other the tube works at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Company's works. Ultimately the choice of the meeting fell upon Mr. Walker, who was elected by a large mljonty. Messrs. John Roberts, T, Burton, and B. Wadsworth were elected trustees of the committee fund. •

div.head: RN. H. Illinica's Contralotion of The Act.
div.p: The RN. H. Illinica's Contralotion of The Act.
" invading the Realms of Conseienn." " Ethicational Efficiency Sacrifind to Sectarian Ends."

The Rev. Herbert Dunnico preached a sermon in criticism of the Education Act at Golborne -street Baptist Church on Sunday evening. Basing his remarks on Luke 20, ver. 23 "Render therefore unto Cmsar the things thatare Csar's, but unto God the things which belong to God," the preacher said that in these words the Master had laid down a law for all people for all time. The claims of Csar were real and imperative so long as Cxsar remained in his proper sphere: it was

unchriaian to refuse to recognizethOseclaims but there was a realm where Cesar had no right to intrude, the realm where God alone had a right to reign and if ; Cesar intruded within those realms he must be resisted at all cost. Some men like Mr. Arthur Balfour were asking • "How is it that Nonconformists feel so I strongly upon this Education Act that such men as Clifford or McLaren, Professor Massie and others have decided to adopt such an extreme method of opposition, as passive 'resistance." The reply was— for conscience sake. Cesar is asking for that which belongs to God, we cannot obey we are prepared to give toCissar the things which belong to him but we will not and cannot give him the things which belong to God. He (the preacher) was prepared to admit that such a method of ; resistance could not be tolerated for one single moment on purely political grounds, but it was because they realised that this question touched upon religions ; grounds that they were -prepared to take their stand dis- regardless of all consequences. This act invaded the realms of conscience. A new andhigher law than the litw of England came into Operation and they would be false to their owe he-Lets and traitors to their country if they submitted without protest. How far was this act calculated to promote or murder national education? He further spoke upon that, aspect of the act asa citizen and as a working man. He must confess he viewed it with Many misgivings. The act had a curious distinc- tion of its own the like of -which he hoped he would never see again. It was a civil measure with a denomi- national purpose, it was so vague and indefinite that the authors did not understand it but two things which it was clear upon were these :—vie., it abolished Board Schools and placed denominational schools upon the rates. What did the abolition of Board Schools mean? It meant that a system of education which had done more than any other to promote elementary education —and which would have done more had it not been for the bitter , opposition of the clergy— was now a thing of the past. In the year 1898, 325 junior scholarships were awarded in London elementary sch4ols and 5 out of every 6 were won by children in Board schools. Those figures were a fair criterion of the respective merits of the voluntary schools and Board schools. They were more ably managed, better adapted for teaching purposesenore efficiently manned, produced betterlresults. They tolerated no distinctively denomi- national teaching. They were governed directly by the pee* and for the nee of the people who Paid tosepport them and yet the government by one fell stroke has 'destroyed them. What had they given in their place? They had passed a Bill which sacrificed educational efficiency to sectarian and priestly ends and which vio- lated the principle of civil and religions liberty. The great principle of popular control had also been end it had roused the opposition not only of Noncon- formists, bet of trades and labour councils, in factor all men who had any regard for justice and fair play. No Bill could receive his assent which withdrew power from the hands of the people who provided the means. The extension and not the extinction of the Board school was what was needed. He believed that ; ere long they would have a system of education, national free without sectarian bias where the children should meet as the sons and daughters of citizens and not as the peppits and implements of priestly arrogance, clerical intolerance and sectarian bigotry. Mr. Fred Monks had said in his hearing is short time ago that this Education Act was one of the greatest strides in educational reform Yet taken. He regretted that he could not share Mr. Monks expectations. He was very much afraid it was a beautiful dream. Either Mr. Monks had not studied the Act or he kept back half the truth. He did not tell them that henceforth the teaching profession in one half the schools in the country would be closed against, all those who would not submit ton religious test. The preacher then pro- ceeded to dismiss the avowed (Neat of these sectarian schools and upon which the Nonconfornist opposition este chiefly based. The Acterocently passed placed all Voluntary schools upon the rates whilst it confined the appointment of teachers to members of that denomina- tion. He had more contempt for a Wesleyan a Baptist or a Congregationalist who availed himself of this Act in order to teach his own distinctive tenets than he had for a Romanist oran Anglican. The Sectarian schools though maintained by the state were to be virtually under the control of the church and clergy to which they belonged and he need not say what would be the result. The avowed object of those church sehools was not only to give definite instruction in the religious prin- ciples of the particular church to which it belonged at a certain part of the day, but it was to create a certain atmosphere which one Bishop had described as a "Catholic atmosphere" and which another Bishop had described as "being poisonous to Nonconformity." Of what use was a conscience clause in such a system of education as that. The Dean of St.. .Paul's had said that parents should be made to naderstand that if their children were only receiving instruction in the scriptures they were not, in any proper sense of the word, receiv- ing religious instruction at all.. Could he have said more plainly that the religious teaching given in clerical schools was not the teaching of the Bible or of Christ or of the Apostles, but of the Priest. Mr. Thymic° then gave several illustrations of the kind of teaching in which it was . said that the first Noncon- formist of all was the Devil and said that if that did not rouse all the opposition a man was capable of he did not know what' would. Before they would submit to that they would submit to be "hung, burnt, sold up." Yes like the old puritan who was brought upbefore a Bishop for tripl they would say, "Ye may have power to hang us hut know ye not we have power to be hanged and defy ye." In all fairness however he ought to make his posi- tion clear. As 'a Nonconforniist he believed in perfect toleration much as he detested their teachings, appeehensive as he was for the welfare of anation where each doctrines were taught, yet if an Anglican or a Romanist desired his children to be trained in such an titmosPhere as that referred to, they were at liberty to have their wish gratified, but on one condition—let him pay for it, let him, not, ask Nonconformists to pay for stich teaching wherein his children were taught to des- pise the faith of his fathers.—Tn conclusion the Preacher made an earnest appeal to the yonng men and women who were there in such large numbers to beware of priest craft, to cherish heirliberties ; to fight for free- dom. If they wished to demoralise and degrade human chaplets; ; to rivet the fetters of superstition, and breathe ghostly terror into the hearts of the people, thee let them pot the educative' of the children into the hands of the priest. The priest has ever been the enemy of freedom and liberty. If they wish to see what secrelotalism would do let them visit Ireland. /relate/ the land of loveliest skies, of noble manhood and Womanhood was Iyi eg hopelessly ruined, not because of the political tyranny of England, but because of the priestly tyranny of Rome Trollied would long since have broken the tyranny With- out if she heti not been broken herself by powerful tyranny Within. Let them go to Ttaly,once rich in the arts of life,graces of intellect. Her day is pasther sceptre has departed, one-third of her children are born out of wedlock. Let them go to Spin the land of the cruel inquisition, likewise France and they would see what England would become if the priest gets ihto power. The essence of Priestism was corruption. it never changed. it is ee bitter to-day as ever and the fires of Smithfield would be relit if they. had noNser. Our fathers were heroic men, bravely they lived, nobly they died. Ti) save our land from corruption and win it for Christ was their motto. Ours must not be less. Ti • conclusion the preacher said :—Rise then in the strength of your manhood. Rise in the beauty of your woman- hood, let them in the words of Sohn Peury the Welsh
martyr, exclaim :—" TI my blood were an ocean and every drop thereof was a life to me T would giye them all for the nriintainance of my confession."

div.head: RUNCORN CONSTABLES' ANNUAL SOCIAL.
div.p: RUNCORN CONSTABLES' ANNUAL SOCIAL.

On Weda?-4lay evening at the Primitive Methodist school, the Runcorn Police Constable held theirannual social. The room had been very tastefully decorated by Mr. T. Wood, streamers, bannerettes, and mottoes. being hung from the . ceiling and walls. •At six o'clock about sixty "of the force" with their wiveg and sweethearts sat down to a most substantial repast prepared by Mesdames S. Coventry, T. Wood and S. Cooke. After tea a capital programme was submitted, the following artistes taking part :—Messrs. Naylor, P. Kenwright, J. Robinson, R. Morris, T. Yates, A. Grounds, S. Ennion, W. Shaw, Mrs. Ennion, Miss E.•Turner,Mies Simkin, Miss Timperley and W. Cooks, F.R.C.O. (accompanist.) Superintendent Ennion presided, and in opening the meeting said that he felt it a great honour at being asked to take the chair on suchan occasion. He would rather have seen Mr. Norman in the position—as last year—and he was sorry he could not be with them that evening. He would not take up the time, because he did not pretend to be it speech-maker, but he would like to thank those who took such interest in the Constabulary as to inaugurate apoliceman's social. He- was sure they would he rewarded by knowing that they intended to thoroughly enjoy themselves. Since the last social there had been many police changes in Run- corn. Some had been transferred to other divisions. He was proud to know there was one among them who had retired on a pension. (Applause). He hoped there Would be many more who would be able to follow his example. He would like to say that his term in Runcorn had been the most pleasant part of his life as a policeman. He had always found the. Runcorn people ready to help him ill the discharge of his duty, and also in other ways as shown by the donors. (Applause.) After the entertainment progressive games were in- dulged in, after which supper was partaken of. The committee responsible for the arrangements con- sisted of Messrs. S. Coventry, S. Wood. and J. Cooke upon whom the greatest credit devolves for the satis- factory manner in which the event was organized and carried out, _ _

At the conclusion of the social, Inspntor Egerton proplsed, Inspector Naylor of Chester, seconding avoto of thanks to the donors, to the committee responsible for the arrangements and to the ladies who had presided at the table. Messrs. Wood, Coventry and Cooke replied, the latter mentioning that there was a deficit of 13s. Gd. on the social last year. All the magistrates were agreed that the object was a, worthy one. The following is the list of donors :—Sir R. Brooke, Messrs. T. Taylor, F. A. Prost, P. J. Norman, A. R. Norman, Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., E. Tmison, W. Thnmins, J. Pritchard. •

div.head: IMPORTANT TO ALL.
div.p: IMPORTANT TO ALL.

Every person's future is, to a certain extent, in his own hand. Many a future which might have been brilli: ant has been darkened by lack of the spirit of self-help. Many a home, which' might have been gladdened by life and health; and comfort, has been saddened by poverty, illness, and death, in many cases wholly preventible. The spring and summer months are, from a sanitary point of view, among the -most important of the year. Due care may now mean a healthy and happy summer and autumn, and robust constitution to meet the trials of next winter. Neglect may now mean a joyless summer, a trying autumn, and a broken constitution to succumb under the attacks of any exceptional trial. There are, indeed, few that do not feel the system needs recruiting after the trying Ns-hater they have passed through. With some it is "only h little cough," with others, "a tendency to bronchitis," with others " not quite up to the mark," "a sort of all-over sinking feeling," "to weak to do anything about the house," "these recurring headaches," "no appetite for my food," etc. These and a dozen others are common expressions, which all point to the urgent need of.some good tonic. What change of air can do for you .in a few months time—if you are no worse than you are now—a course of some good tonic mixture, a reliable medicine of established reputation and of proved virtue will do now. BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Minor Cases, Warrington Borough Pollee Court.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Messrs. Hepherd and Thornton. INCORRIGIRLIL—A boy named Richard William Gregory, of 224, Knutsford-road, was summoned for be- ing found wandering and not under proper control.— Mr. W. Jones, school attendance inspector, said the boy was quite incorrigible and had got beyond the control of his mother, who was a widow. He was continually on the streets and never went to school.—The Bench ordered the boy to be sent to Ardwick Green Industrial School until he is 1.6 years of age. WIFE DESERTION.—John Monks, Gorsey-lane, was summoned for deserting his wife, Ellen Monks.—Mr. Browne appeared for the compininant and Mr. Steel defended.—The desertion was adinitted and the Bench granted a separation order with 6s. per week alimony. UNUSUAL COURSE ADOPTED.—The magistrates • felt justified in adopting an unusual course in th 6 case of ,Thomas Barry who was charged on remand with being an absentee from the Yorkshire and Lancashire Regiment stationed at Pontefract.—Prisoner was before the court on Thursday, when he explained that he would shortly be going on service abroad and he came to Warrington without obtaining leave in order to see his father. He was remanded in custody to await the arrival of an escortbnt yesterday morning Superintendent Monaghan said the escort had not yet arrived and his only course ' was to ask for another remand.—Prisonersaid he would go to Pontefract by himself if the Bench would liberate him. Ultimately the magistrates decided •to release him on bail, on his promising to appear again this morn- lug. They did not consider it right that he should be kept in custody another day

31!).);DAY.—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, and Messrs. Hayward, Vright and Thornton. STUCK IN THE MUD.—Martin Shaughnessy, who is 70 years of age, and resides at 9, Dial-street, was charged with being drunk and incapable at Arpley on night.—Police Constable Howard was on duty near the Iron Bridge when he heard someone shouting for help. He proceeded along the river side and found the prisoner fast in the mud below the river bank. He got him out and found that he was drunk. If the tide had been up he might have been drowned.—Superin- tendent Monaghan stated that the pri ioner had not been before the Court previously, and with the permission of the Bench he would withdraw the case.—Prisoner was discharged. GAMBLING.—Five beys, named Harold Braide, 8, 'Melville-street ; Thomas McDonoghne, 1, Melville- street ' • Thomas Hayes, 4, Watkin-street ; William Whittaker, 107, Longford-street, and Charles Watson, 2:2, Warburton-street, were summoned for tossing for money in Melville-street on March Bth.—P.C. Lewis proved the case.—Braide, Whittaker, and Watson, the elder defendants, were fined ss. each, and the others each.

St.7;DAY NIGHT DISORDER.--Four young men named Robert McCarthy, 17, Warburton-street; Harry McCarthy, 17, Warburton-street ; Joseph Barker 27, Warburton-street, and William Jaundrell, Jockey-street were each fined ss. and costs, on the evidence of P.O Dyson, for making loud and unseemly noises in Long- ford-street, at half-past eleven on SundSy night, March Sth.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Patrick Carey, 42,Dallam lane, and Thoma-s Ellison, 3, Dial-court, who committed a breach of the peace by fighting in Houghton-street on March sth, were bound over to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay the costs is. each.—For making use of obscene language in Erwood-street on March Bth, John Emmett, 23, Erwood-street was fined ss.

ThEsDAY.—Before Aldermen Shaw Green (presiding), and Hutchinson and Dr. Pox. SSTRUGGLE WITH A PRISONER.—AIbert Snelson, atevenson-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Rodney-street at 12.5 that morning zul with assaulting P.C. Clarke.—The constable said he ound the prisoner lying on his back in the middle of the road. He got the man on his feet and prisoner after asking him if he could "use his fists" struck him in ithe face. Prisoner was very violent and after struggling with him to the Fire Station witness blew his whistle and P.C. Whitby came to his assistance. Prisoner was then taken to the lock-up.---A flit) of 10s. and costs with the alternative of 14 days imprisonment Was inflicted.

Local DruldiEra. The 'quarterly meeting of the " Druids Camp Lodge " of the Order of Druids was held at the Higher Angel Inn, Buttermarket-street, on Saturday evening. The business was cniducted by the district officers, and there was a crowded attendance. Grand Master Bro. Ray presided. , Vice Grand Master Bro. John Bibby was in the vice-chair, Bro. Eden, D.T., filling the office of P.J.N.G.A. and D.C.S. Bro. Hough- ton supported the lodge secretary, Bro. - Paker. Several new members were initiated and the general business was gone through. The Grand Master, in making the presentation of a silver medallion of the order, on behalf of the district, to Bro. William Hankey for the services he had rendered to the lodge by introducing so many new members during the past three months, said it was a unique experience, and one that he hoped would be repeated not only in that \ lodge, but in other lodges in the district, as two mem- bers were to receive marks of appreciation from the district for services rendered on one night.--The Vice Grand Master then made Bro. Charnley a present of one of the medallions, and expressed the hope that the good work he had began would be continued and that he would aspire to higher offices in connection -with the order. He felt sure it would not be long before the district at least would bestow more favour upon him. (Applause.)—Bro. D. Houghton, D.C.S., joined in the«. pleasure it afforded' the district to render honour to whom honour was due and to testify from time to time their appreciation of services rendered , such as had. been displayed by their two brothers. Bros. Hankey and Charnley thanked the district for their handsome g.: fts and the officers for attending to make the pr*sentations. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the officers and visiting brethren. Songs recitations, readings, and phonograph pieces were given by various members and added to the enjoy- ment of the proceedings.

div.head: APOLLO CHOIRS' CONCERT.
div.p: THE APOLLO CHOIRS' CONCERT.

Efforts to cultivate local musical talent are always to be welcomed, and those townspeople who are anxious Warrington shall hold its ownan this respect, will hail with satisfaction the formation of a second Apollo Choir. Hitherto the name Apollo as applied to a body of vocalists in Warrington has denoted a male voice choir only. Encouraged by the success which has attended that organization from the outset, the com- mittee decided upon the formation of a mixed choir. The requisite number of female voices has been forth- coming, and the choir nowhas a membership of seventy, forty of whom also constitute the Male Voice Choir. Considerable interest centred in the first public appearance of the mixed choir at the con- cert held in the Parr Hall on Monday even- ing, which was the second concert promoted this season by the Apollo choir. Considering the fact that the concert season is fast drawing to a close, and that Warringtonians have been exceptionally well catered for as regards entertainments during the past few months, the attendance was highly satisfactory, most parts of the hall being comfortably filled. From'a musical point of view the concert was a complete success, an unusually attractive programme be submitted in a manner which not onlyreflected credit upon the artistes but called forth the unstinted approbation of the aud- ience. The mixed choir created a very favourable itn- pression. There was an intelligent co-operation on the part of all the members, and the voices blended admir- ably. The interpretations of "Mariners," "Hush, my child" and "Lord of the waves" were marked by very careful attention to expression, and it was evident that no pains had been spared to bring the choir to a state of proficiency. Mr.-Thomas Brough wielded the baton and to his able guidance the success attained by the choir on its first public appearance was in a great measure due. The audience so appreciated the singing that two encores were accorded. The male voice choir fully maintained its reputation, "Crossing the plains" affording ample scope for the display .of the talents which have stood them in ' such good stead in various competitions. The beautiful part song "The long day closes" was given with equal success. The promoters of the con- cert were very fortunate in their selection of solo artistes, the remainder of the programme being sustained by Miss Lizzie Skeet (soprano), Miss Backsheen Wood (solo violin), Mr. Harry Berrey (tenor), Mr. Arthur Weber (bass) and Mr. Lindon Wyatt (humorist), each of whom has been heard in Warrington before. Miss Lizzie Skeet possesses a ' rich and flexible voice, and gave charming interpretations of "Kathleen Mavourneen," and "Come back to me." The pleasure of the audience was expressed by loud and prolonged applause, and Miss Skeet responded to recalls with sweet interpretations of "a little bit of string" and the ever- green "Killarney," Miss Backsheen Wood's abilities as a violinist are well-know to local concert-goers. Her playing on Monday evening was characterised by brilliant execution and refinement of expression and called forth the highest encomiums, the accomplished performer responding to two encores. Mr. Harry Berrey is the possessor of a pure-toned tenor voiceand was responsible for an effective rendering of " The last watch.' A hearty encore was responded to with" Come into the garden Maud" and later in the evening Mr. Berrey sang "When other lips "in creditable style. Mr. Arthur Weber is a favourite With Warrington audiences and he was accorded a great ova- tion. His • deep-toned and powerful voice was heard to perfection in all his songs, Mr. Weber's ability to find the lower notes being perhaps most clearly demonstrated in "Rocked in the cradle of the deep" which he sang on being encored for an expressive interpretation of "In sheltered vale." He had the honour of another vigorous recall for his interpretation of "The curfew," the meaning of the words being fully brought out, and complied with the request for another sow, with that stirring composition "The boys of the olebrigade." The humorous element was sustained by Mr. Lindon Wyatt who soon established himself as a favourite with he audience. His anecdotes were especially good and he succeeded in keeping his hearers in a very jovial mood. The. Male Voice Choir brought an excellent entertainment to a close with a "Laughing chorus." A mood of praise is due to the accompanists, Messrs. E Wilkes, A.L.C.M. andA. Trow who discharged their duties with taste and ability.

Personai. Mr. F. Dunne, of Warrington, has been selected as one of the draughts team to represent England in the International match with Scotland, which is to take place at Newcastle, at Easter. The Town Clerk of Widnes (Mr. H. S. Oppenheim) has been admitted to the freedom of the Worshipful Company of Cordwainers by patrimony, and has been made a freeman of the eily of London. • Saturday Evening Concerts.

The above series of entertainments .in connection with the 1.0.G.T. Temperance Mission Lodge, were continued in Ebenezer Church on Saturday.- Mr. Metcalf presided and gave a Stirring address on the evils of drink, and gave some startling statistics on the traffic in intoxicating liquor . He compared the cost of the late war and the st of supplying the English nation with drink. Var ous illustrations were given of the speaker's own knowledge of the evils of intemperance. Selections were given on a gramophone kindly lent by Mr'. W. Hudson and . manipulated by Mr. J. Sheath. Miss C. Jackson was very successful in the rendering of" Will he no' come back. again." A recitation entitled " The little housemaid " was rendered by Miss Jane Hughes. Messrs Rigby and Aukland caused a great deal of amusement by a cleverly presented humorous sketch. Miss G. Hughes recited " Comrade Jim " (a story of the battle of Grasp* with good effect. The meeting oncluded with the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: DETECTION CERTAIN.
div.p: DETECTION CERTAIN.
THERE IS NO POISON TO-DAY THAT CANNOT BE TRACED.
Thrilling Stories of Poisoners Crimes.

Chapman is only a clumsy poisoner after all. That snap of his thumb and finger and that statement of his to the sister of his last victim, Maud Marsh, that he could "give her a dose Which fifty doctors could not discover," exhibits the depth of his ignorance of modern scientific analysis, and the wantonness of his criminal folly. It forged an important link in the chain of evidence which hands over a depraved murderer to the common hangsman. The truth is that there is no poison to-day the administration of which to a human subject cannot be traced, and in this fact lies the public safety.

div.head: UNSCIENTIFIC MURDERER.
div.p: THE UNSCIENTIFIC MURDERER.

_ Tartar emetic was the agent by which Chapman remaved his three victims, but the quantities he administered were so entirely enormous, so vastly in excess of a fatal dose, that not only was suspicion aroused in the mind of alniost every witness in attend- ance on the unfortunate women, by the violence of the sickness and purging, bu“he organs of the victims after death were also found to be.saturated with poison.

div.head: TYPICAL CASE.
div.p: A TYPICAL CASE.

Now here is a typical case: The subject becomes unexpectedly and critically ill. She dies with signs and symptoms that agree with those produced by the administration of a well-known mineral poison. This poison is found in her body after death, and the possession of it is traced to the indivipal suspected. If now the suspected man can be shown to have any reason for desiring the removal of the victim the story is com- plete. The typical case, it will be seen, applies to Chapman.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC MEDICAL POISONER.
div.p: THE SCIENTIFIC MEDICAL POISONER.

Chapman's conviction recalls quiteanumber of others well within the recollection of middle-aged readers of this column. They will remember the Lamson case. In this case it was shewn that the doctor having money interest in the death of a young relative gave him a poisonous dose of aconite enclosing .it in a oapsule with some white sugar. He selected his opportunity carefully for the boy who was in delicate health had just made a full meal of the kind which might be expected to induce indigestion. Some hours after swallowing the capsule the unfortunate lad died.. Lamson was a man who had completed a medical education. He was wellacquainted with the ordinary processes of a post mortera examination, and he may be excused for thinking that the fraction of a grain of a poison for which there was no chemical test might escape detection after death particularly when mixed with the contents of a full stomach. It was his fatal error.
TO DEFY CHEMICAL RESEARCH.

Dr. Lamson thought that the symptoms of his poison- ing would in the first place go unrecognised, and in the next that should the death certificate be withheld the agent that he had selected would defy chemical re- search. In identical circumstances he and Chapman thought alike. _ _ _ _

Bu i his belief was ill-founded. Aconite had only once before been investigated in the Law Courts as the cause of death, so that the effects of the drug necessarily could not be within the common knowledg.t. The ordin- ary post .mortent made by direction of the coroner re- vealed no cause of death. But suspicion chanced to fall on Lamson and an enquiry was started With a view to show that the boy had been murdered byttn irritant poison.

div.head: CLUE WHICH HANGED THE DOCTOR.
div.p: CLUE WHICH HANGED THE DOCTOR.

The clue was obtained from a few words that fell from .the dying boy in which he complained of some peculiar sensations in his mouth and throat. Scientific evidence confirmed the suspicions from two acts of experiments conducted by experts upon themselves and upon mice— by injections of the fluid taken from the dead boy's stomach. This fluid extract had the taste to the ex- erts of symptoms always associated with the use of aconite and described by the boy when dying. Further the .fluid killed mice in a certain time with certain signs and these signs and times were identical with other sign's and times produced when mice were killed with solutions coutainingaconite of a known strength.

div.head: MAAKED MAN.
div.p: A MAAKED MAN.

This was held to be proof that the boy had died of aconite poisoning. Then it was proved that Lamson had bought aconite in more than one place and had tried to buy it in others. The infrequency of the use of aconite in ordinary medicine and its known deadly properties made Lamson's purchases memorable And he was a marked man in half-a-dozen druggists' shops with- out having personal knowledge of the fact. Pecuniary gain being also shown to lesult to him from the death of the boy he was hanged, and the reason was his ignor- ance. He knew really less than the Home Office ex- perts.

CONVICTED BY A DROP OF WATER. A case is recorded in medical history which if he had acquainted himself with it would have saved Chapman his neck, and his victims their lives. In this case con- viction was secured from a drop of water in a phial. It was all that was left of some drinking water prepared by the poisoner to be given to his wife. The bottle ' full of drinking-water was corked and placed by a wit- nesst. in his .trousers' pocket. But the cork came out and the water disappaared. The Win was told to bring the empty bottle for examinatiam, together with the lining of his pocket. The quantity of water left in, the phial was so small that it could not be poured out. It had to be withdrawn by a delicate glass tube. Yet when it was evaporated slowly it disclosed crystals of emetic tartar. Thee were micro-photographed and then metallic antimony was obtained from them. Antimony was also obtained from the strip of the poc- ket lining no longer than a man's finger. •

div.head: CASE OF FLORENCE MA YBRICK.
div.p: THE CASE OF FLORENCE MA YBRICK.

The crime of Florence Maybrick sentenced to death in 1889, but respited, for causing the death of her husband by the administration of excessive doses of arsenic obtained from fly, papers, is well in the public mind, owing to the frequent newspaper references made to it. In this case the symptoms were excessive sickness, purging, pain in the abdomen, more marked in the pit of the stomach, and cramps in the calves of the legs. The motive was alleged to be that which is common when a young pretty woman stoops to a liaison. '
POISONED BY STRYCHNINR AND ARSENIC.

Half-a-dozen other cases of poisoning are recalled by Chapman's conviction. Few, newspaper readers will for- get the fate of Walter Horsford, the young Spalding farmer who caused the death of Mrs. Annie Holmes, a 'young widow and his cousin, in 1893, by the administra- tion of strychnine. Not all the eloquence of Mr. Ernest E. Wild, made more famous in the recent sensational Peasenhall double trial, saved Horsford front the hangs- man. Catherine Flannagan and Margaret Higgins were executed at Liverpool in 1884 for the murder by poison- ing of Thomas Higgins the husband of the latter with arsenic. They also poisoned three other persons, their object being to secure the payment of not /ess than £lOO the amount of insurances effected on their lives. These cases resembled in certain respects the Chapman case; in the exhumation of the victims' bodies; in their wonderful state of preservation, in the saturation of the organs with repeated overdoses of poison, and in deceiv- ing the medical man in attendance upon Thomas Higgins as to death.

div.head: BALH A M MYSTERY RECALLED.
div.p: THE BALH A M MYSTERY RECALLED.

The case of Mr. Charles Delaney Bravo, barrister, 5 of The Priory, Balham which caused such a sensation in the seventies and touched the reputation of some men and women prominent in the eye of the public, was a case of antimonial poisoning. After two.enquiries the second a protracted and painful one, the jury found that Mr. Bravo met his death by tartar emetic. They put it on record that he did not take this deadly poison, by misadventure, and that he did not commit suicide, and that as al matter of fact he was wilfully murdered. But there was no charge and therefore no conviction in what was and still is described as "The Balham Mystery."

div.head: IDENTITY OF "JACK:.THE-RIPPER.4
div.p: IDENTITY OF "JACK:.THE-RIPPER.4

Thomas Neill alais Cream, a dissolute and debased drug agent with a medical knowledge whom well in- formed official opinion credits with the "Jack-the- Ripper "horrors, was banged in London in November, 1892 for the murder by the administration of poison of Matilda Glover en unfortunate. He gave hi % victim strychnine in a capsule and he is believed to' have poisoned three other girls with whom he made acquain- tance, and whose deaths could not otherwise be ex- plained. A .young woman named Harris swore at the trial that he tried to administer capsules to. her but that by a little sleight \of hand she had without the knowledge of Cream avoided swallowing them. Neill told several people that this girl had died from poison- ing when as a matter of fact she was alive and well, and coming forward as a witness at the preliminary investi- gation of the este she destroyed the last lingering possibility of the prisoner's innocence.
P(.I,ONED WIFE. MARRIED GOVERNESS.

Dr. Philip Cross was hanged in Cork in January 1888 for the murder of his wife by the administration of arsenic. There had never previously been a trial for wife murder which had created such intense interest in the South of Ireland. Dr. Cross who was a retired Surgeon-major in the Army came off a well 'known County family. He married in August 1869. Mary Laura Marriott,a young lady who brought him a fortune of £5,000. He formed the acquaintance of Miss Skinner, a governess,and was found sharing quarters with her ma Dublin Hotel. He became indifferent to his wife and on the 18th May 1887 the unfortunate woman was found 'to be exhibiting symptoms of arsenical poisoning. She had excessive sickness and diarrhcea and through the month find in June following these symptoms:re-appeared and finally she died under circumstances which excited the gravest suspicion. Two days later the funeral took place, the husband certifying that death resulted from typhoid fever. In the -following week Dr. Cross left tqr London and married the governess at St. James's Church, Piccadilly. The marriage increased local sits- picion. The wife's body was exhumed, the organs were found to be saturated with arsenic and Dr. Cross met: his fate "with firmness and fortitude" according to Cork history. PARSON'S WIFE POISONING RUSE.

One other case of arsenical poisoning is perhaps not without interest in connection with Chapman's convic- tion. A druggist made an affidavit that a clergyman in Jersey City after learning from him the properties of emetic tartar and after inspecting a bottle with its latin label called on two separate occasions when no cus- tomers were in the shop and asked for a book or pamphlet which obliged him to go to a room upstairs. The parson then stole the poison and administered it to his wife. He was convicted.
