div.head: Examiner, Friday, March 20, 1903. LOCAL ODDFELLOWSHIP I FASHIONS OF TO-DX. Presentation to Past Grand Thomas , Wadsworth. A Creditable Record of Service.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, March 20, 1903. LOCAL ODDFELLOWSHIP I FASHIONS OF TO-DX. Presentation to Past Grand Thomas , Wadsworth. A Creditable Record of Service.

There was a large muster of Odd*lows at the Pelican Hotel, Buttermarket-street,on Thlisday last[week, when a social gathering was held for the purposeaf making a presentation to Past Grand Thomas Wadsworth, in recbgnition of the valuable services rendered by him during the past twenty-one years as secretary of the Prince of Wales Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity). Past Grand Wadsworth is held in the highest esteem by his brother Oddfellows who greatly appreciated his ungrudging and succeasful efforts to promote the prosperity of the lodge. The gift took the form of a very handsome case of cutlery, and several speeches eulogising the work of Past Grand Wadsworth were delivered. The chair was occupied by N. G. Thomas P. .Bradshaw, who was supported by Prov. G. M. Ellis R. Clare, Prov. D.G.M.R. H. Holford, Prov. C. S. Frank Webster, P.P.G.M's Massey, J. H. Norbury,Thomas S. Steel, Gilbert Riley, S. Baldry, and M. Knowles, P.G's, Fred Taylor, William Holbrook William Owen, William Houghton. William Bibby, d. F. Freeman, Horrabin, . Henry Lawrence, Wilkinson, Hough, Joseph Taylor, and N. Sumner' and officers and members of the various lodges in the district. There were also present P.P.G.M. George Wilkins, of Liver- pool(who made the presentation) andthe Prov. D.G.M. of Liverpool, Bro. Walsh. The CHAIRMAN, before asking P.P.G.M. Wilkins to make the presentation said they had met to give honour to whom honour was due. The presentation was in recognition of the valuable services rendered to the Prince of \Vales lodge during the past twenty-one years by its secretary, Past Grand Wadsworth. He found that Brother Wadsworth joined the lodge in 1878, and was appointed secretary in 1881. At that time the member- ship of the lodge was 168, the average age of the mem- bers being 37-1 years, and the funds in hand amounted to £921. During his term of office the lodge had advanced numerically and financially and they now had a membership of about 450. The average age had been reduced by seven years and the funds in hand amounted to £2,556 3s. Under Brother Wadsworth's able guidance the Lodge had made very much headway. It was aow in a very sound position which it could not have attained if it had not had a man at the head of affiairs so strong and capable of managing the affairs of the lodge as the Secretary. The figures he had referred to would be a credit to any Secretary in the Order. The present was accompanied by the best wishes of the lodge for Bro. Wadsworth's future and the members hoped and trusted that they would have his valuable services for -many years to come. In that case they would fearnothing. (Applause.) -- P.P.G.M.!—Willkins, in making the presentation,, referred to Past Grand Wadsworth's desire for financial reform in connection with the lodge. He found from the information supplied to him that Bro. Wadsworth almost immediately he became secretary set to work to improve the- condition of the lodge financially. That condition had now greatly improved, and he believed he was correct instating that the deficiency which Brother. Wadsworth found when he took charge of the funds of the lodge had now been decreased by one half. He had very little doubt, Considering the manner in which the funds were invested, the contributions they paid, and Ithe watch they kept over sick and funeral expenditure, that when the next valuation took place the lodge would be on the right side instead of the wrong side, and have a surplus rather than a deficiency. Bro. Wadsworth was not long in the lodge before he made his mark. Be- fore becoming secretary he had passed through various offices, and was a Past Grand when he was elected financial secretary. That, he thought, showed that Bro. Wadsworth very early indeed earned the confidence of the brethren of the lodge because undoubtedly the members of a lodge even of the size of the Price of Wales lodge at the time would look round very anxiously before they placed the management of the financial affairs of the lodge in the hands of any brother. The speaker referred to the services rendered by Bro. Wadsworth to other local organizations and said the members admired the 'pluck and industry of Bro. AWadsworth in undertaking so many duties. His work had not been done with the object of getting a present,but simply for the good of the Order. It afforded him (the speaker) the greatest possible pleasure to be the medium of the Prince of Wales lodge in ask- ing Bro. Wadsworth's acceptance of the very handsome case of cutlery as an evidence of the good feeling which the members still retained towards him. It spoke volumesi for Bro Wadsworth's character that after having sometimes had to tell the members unplyasant truths during his term of office, they should feel so kindly disposed towards him as to make the presenta- tion. He hoped Bro Wadsworth would be spared for very many years to use the articles and to give more work than he had already 'given to the Prince of lodge to the Warrington district, and to the Manchester Unity. (Applause.) P.P.G.M. MASSEY endorsed Bro. Wilkins' remarks and said the amount of energy that Bro. Wadsworth bie thrown into his work for the Order was incalcula • (Applause.) P.G. Bibby, who the CHAIRMAN said, was Brother Wadsworth's opponent when the election of -secretary took place, said the lodge made a wise selection in appointing Bro. Wadsworth, who was one of the finest secretaries in England. (Hear, hear.) When he took over the duties Oddfellowship was not in a good con- dition locally, owing to the amalgamation of the old Victoria lodge and the Prince of Wales lodge which were in a pool. position. The result of Bro. Wadsworth's work had been a marvel to him. (Applause.) Bro. HEDGECOCK also spoke. Bro. WADSWORTH, who was received with. the sing- ing of "For he's a jelly good fellow" and cheers, said a great deal had been said with reference to the time and trouble he had given to the work, but he could assure them that the work had always been a pleasure to him, for when they came to consider that during his period of office there had been distributed in sick pay alone £3,700, they must know that in very many cases the money must have been very acceptable—in fact it was impossible to realise the benefit it must have been to their members. They had also been able to add £1,700 to their capital. In no single year had the lodge gone back either numerically or financially. They felt proud of the position it had attained, which must stand out favourably when compared with any other lodge in the Unity. He did not wish for a momentto take credit for the success attained, for it was not through the efforts of one or two individuals that such results could have been brought about, but by the united efforts of the officers and members generally. He was pleased to say they had among them a large:number of !members who con- sidered nothing was too much trouble to do for thea benefit of their cause. Bro. Wadsworth referred to the valuable services rendered by the trustees in regard to the investment of the funds, and remarked that he had no hesitation in saying that if the same care was exercised in the future as- had been exercised in the past, no member need have fear that the lodge would not always be able to discharge its full liabilities to its members. After thanking the officers and members for their assistance, Bro. Wadsworth concluded by assuring the members that his work in the future would be

done, as it had been done in the past with the object of watching the interests of the lodge and its members. (Applause). A'hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Liver- pool brethren for their attendance. During the evening a very enjoyable musical programme was submitted, P.G. Ffr Webster discharging the duties of accompanist. Songs were rendered by Brothers Freeman, Healing, Atherton, Emson, Reddish, Boyle, and Earle and Bro. Massey recited. The following committee had had charge of the arrangements :—Brothers J. H. Norbury, P.P.G.M., J. Massey, P.P.G.M., F. Webster, P.G., D. Whitham, P.G., T. P. Bmdshaw,N.G.(trea.surer)and G. F. Freeman, P.G. (secretary.)

Benefit Concert. A very successful and enjoyable concert was given in the Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Methodist Mission Room on Saturday evening by Mr. H. H. Taylor and party, in aid of one of the lady teachers who met with an accident some ten months ago, in consequence of which she is confined to her room. There was a large attendance. The proceedings wer3, opened by the audience singing: two verses of the well-known hymn, " All hail the power of Jesus' Name," and prayer offered by Mr*Ellison, after which the pro- gramme was capitally rendered, the following ladies and gentlemen taking,paft in it :—The Misses Alice Longdin, Elsie Taylor, C. 'lasting, and Hartley ; and Messrs. N. R. Silcock, V. Wood, E, R. Hartley, and F. R. Bickford, who were warmly applauded'. The selections on the gramophone were Capitally rendered especially the reproduction of the famous Sousa's band, which called forth rounns of applause. The accompanist was Miss Taylor. A very hearty vote Of thanks was accorded to Mr. H. H. Taylor and his' party, for their kindness on the motion of Mr Gregson, seconded by Mr. Howard.

The newest skirts are much more elaborate than those of last season, and everywhere knife-pleating is a feature of the most fashion- able varieties. The length of the skirt is decided by the nature of the occasion for which it is destined. There is some variation in the manner in which the pleating is ar- ranged, and for accordion or knife-pleating, accordion-box-pleating is substituted wi th excellent effect, and is indeed very muct prettier than the older-fashioned style. The pleats, which are wide towards the pottom of the skirt, diminish to nothing at the waist, this being a matter of great im- portance to all those who are inclined to stoutness below the waist, and to whom an extra fold or two of material is of much im- portance.

Another way of getting over the vexed question of retaining a fashionable slimness below the waist, and yet exploiting the much-pleated skirt, is to have the uppet part of the skirt made with a shaped hip empiecement, from which, the pleats spring.
;TUME,
slender figure can, of course, take the in- creased bulkiness that results from having the pleats springing directly from the waist- band.

The vanishing. pleat, however, undoubtedly gives a more graceful line to the generality of figures, and is therefore likely to be very popular during spring and summer. Thin woollen materials, such as fine cloth or voile, lend themselves readily to. pleating ; while, later on, mousseline and linen, together with some of the fashionable varieties of thin canvas, will be much worn treated in this way. . . • .

'the spring-costume depicted is made of a soft open . canvas in a pastel green over chino silk of the same colour, the p%ats vanishing at the waist. It is worn with a smart little coat trimmed with cream-coloured s ilk braidings, and cord and tassels to match. The toque is of the same tone of green as the gown ; it is trimmed with lace, and is finished at the back by a lace cacheoeigne. It . is, perhaps, almost needless for me to remark that although the pleated or full skirt is le dernier en, the plain skirt will not pass from our midst, because the skirt which fits closely yet ..not too tightly round the hips,

div.head: TYPICAL TAILOR-MADE.
div.p: A TYPICAL TAILOR-MADE.
and from thence falls in soft and graceful folds, has proved itself to be so becoming as to have secured a permanent position in our wardrobes.

For morning wear in corijunction with a plain coat there is nothing so comfortable; and its value will also be appreciated on stormy days when an elaborate skirt would be found unmanageable. A • plain skirt also serves to show off embroidery better than any other, and is a good background to scrolls and appliques generally of strapped and stitched silk or velvet.

A tailor-made gown. has lost its original reputation, for tailors now condescend to adopt elaborate styles which a short time ago would have been considered by them as only within the province of a dressmaker. In my second sketch, however, will be seen the charms of what a tailor-made gown proper was and still, I am glad to say, is :onsidered to be by some firms. _ -

It relies on the correctness of cut and fit for success, and is calculated to show off a good figure to better advantage than any Dther mode when entrusted to experienced hands. Indeed, in these days of loose sacque coats and pleated skirts there is something very distinguished about a costume of the style depicted, the original of which was

II built" (I believe that is the correct term) for quite a great lady in the world of dress. The skirt is cut to a convenient walking length, and the sole trimming consists of a little black velvet in the collar. The cos-

tume itself is of fine faced black cloth, lined ' throughout with a bright shade of apple- green silk: Another innovation mtroduced quite recently is the latest belts, which are of the. Romney or directoire style, instead of the narrow-shaped bands so long worn. The 1 first amed stide is softly draped round the wais ,while the latter is staiened and boned, and as a dee.p buckle down the centre of the front. A trimmer look is given to the figure, as the pouching of the blouse or bodice is naturally much reduced in size. These bolts require careful fitting, cutting, and shaping • to be satisfactory. . The pretty blouse s:zetched is made of white crepe de chine of a supple and silky nature. The yoke is glace. while the sleeves, which preserve the outlines • of the upper part of the arms, become voluminous towards the wrists, where they finish in a transparent lace cuff. A cream silk belt of the directoire style, fastened by a dull gold oval bruckle, finishes the waist and looks exceedingly smart. . COQUETTE.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The fashionable world has not yet entered upon the fulness of a brilliant season, and many people of the leisured, and wealthy classes will follow the examples of their Majesties the King and Queen, and shortly go abroad. Even thoge who can only look forward to a brief holiday at Foster, are already making their plans, and arrangements. Whilst the Queen is in Denmark,the King will go for a cruise in the Victoria and Albert, during which his Majesty will, in all probability pay a visit to the King of Portugal at Lisbon. King Ferdinand was first cousin alike to Queen Victoria and the Prince Consort, so that he is a kinsman of King Edward VII. Both monarchs are descendants of the house of Saxe Coburg, which now occupies a foremost place amongst the reigning Houses of Europe, though less than a hundred years ago, its Princes were but riders of petty German duchies.

The Lenten season is not the period of abstinence it used to be and since its beginning, the Court has been most of the time in London. There have been dinner parties and entertainments at Buckingham Palace and their Majesties have frequently dined out, at the houses of ministers and other great personages. The first of the March Courts, for which about one thousand invita- tions were issued,was also a scene of unusual splendour. Court dresses, it is true, have to conform to cer- tain fixed rules as to the style of bodice and length of train, but each toilette has its distinctive feature in style and colour, and the effect on the whole in such a distinguished gathering is one of infinite variety and magnificence.

aenerally speaking shower bouquets were carried by the matrons, and sheafs. by d‘butantes, attending the first Court of the season and roses, malmaisons lilies-of-the-valley, orchids, and white violets, appeared to be =favorite blooms. Instead of satin ribbon, tulle was in many instances employed to tie up "showers" and sheafs alike,the effect, especially when orchids and roses were concern6d, being fairy like. No lady in the Court circle ever carries a bouquet, on these occasions, 'least of all her Majesty, the Queen. Following the example of Queen Victoria, Queen Alexandra has presented her maids of honour--Miss Sylvia Edwards, Miss Mary Dyke, and the twin Misses Vivian—with miniatures of herself, set in diamonds. During the maids' period of waiting, these exquisite ornaments are surmounted by a flat red and white ribbon bow and worn on the left side of the corsage, like a decoration, but at other times they may be donned as a pendent or brooch. Queen Victoria's miniatures were set in a bracelet, and could only be worn in this way by her maids of honour.

The great pearl fishery which will shortly take place off the N.W. coast of Ceylon, is exciting great interest among connoisseurs and experts in jewellery, but that the most successful crop will reduce the cost of really choice gems, is without doubt a forlorn hope. Pearls are, if possible, more fashionable than ever, while emeralds and rubies are still very much more popular than sapphires, this state of affairs being probably due to the fact that the latter appear dark and somewhat dull, by artificial light. Diamonds remain of tiburse, supreme.. .

. The hair is again being dressed high, and fringes have almost reached vanishing point. One or two soft wide waves only are permissible,and the room smooth and shin- ing our tresses are, the. more modish shall we appear. Hair ornaments for evening are very elaborate. Floral wreaths, wings, aigrettes, all are fashionable, while twists of soft ribbon, chiffo'n, or tulle, are still enjoy- ing a wide vogue. A novel idea is that of a true lovers' knot made of wire, covered with gold or silver ribbon, and sewn with tiny sequins. This arranged tiara fashion is very pretty, and most becoming. The short walking skirt well clears the ground all round, and is the regular thing for morning hours. in Paris it is called the" trotteur "costume, and all who value the health-giving exercise of walking, must hope that it has come to star, as the blouse has done. The blouse which has established itself in universal favor, has resisted all attempts on the part of arbiters of feminine fashion,to supersede it,and whatever our fancy may be for trailing garments indows, we can only hope that the short skirt, now that we have once more got it back will make an equally gallant tight for comfort, and common sense.

It is not often that old proverbs will stand the test of modern statistic& but from an examination of 6,000 boys and girls in sEools it appears that there is some truth in some orthe old notions as regards character, and its relation to colour of eyes and hair, the shape and lines of hands, and general features. Conscientious- ness was taken as the index to character, and the statis- tics, furnished the other day by Professor Pearson, at the Royal Institution, tended decidedly to confirm the conclusions of the old philosophers, who regarded dark, and dark eyed people with suspicion. Thus the pro- portion of the keenly conscientious was higher amongst the light eyed than the dark eyed. A comparison between the dark and light coloured in hair also showed the same state of things, whilst as regards temper the advantage was again on the side.of the blondes. In some other respects the statistics did not bear out • ancient traditions, but they were, Professor Pearson said, seldom at variance with them. _ .

A prize of £250 has been offered in Paris to the house- wife, who by her own labour, best supplements the earnings of her husband, which must not be more than £l4O a year. The Frenchpeople are fond of offering and competing for prizes of a novel description, but there is always one way of supplementing the husband's earnings by careful attention to household economy. A shilling saved is a shilling earned,and in middle class homes, the housewife has opportunities for saving many shillings by careful supervision over the larder—much may also be done to keep Wown gas and coal bills, and some people attain this object by offer- ing a small present to the cook, or general maid,if those do not exceed certain fixed limits.

Owing to the notoriety it has achieved in the Caven- dish case, the planehette, or little woodenefortune- teller, is once more a popular form of entertainment at evening parties. No doubt there are people who be- lieve that it possesses latent powers of communicatinc, with the spirit world, and amongst this class, the planchette is capable of working a good deal of mis- chief, but if approached in the proper spirit of fun, it affords much harmless amusement. Some of the most charming stories have been written about gems or treasures which have been supposed to possess certain spiritual or angelic qualities, but though there are people who would believe anything, it is a little too much to make such a claim for the little wooden article which is turned out,at variops prices, by the gross in a factory, and that in all probability a German manu- factory. . _
MADGE.

On Tuesday a terrible colliery accident was reported to the East Denbighshire coroner. It seems that a number of men were engaged working in a certain part «f the Pins Power Colliery, near Wrexham, when a tre- mendous fall of roof took place, and two men, named Thomas Davies,aged 36, of 10,Penrhos Cottagee,l3rymbo and William Roberts, aged 39, of 13, Brook-terrace,Tany Vron, Brymbo, were killed instantaneously.

The Forthcoming Horse Parade. • i A. statement of the receipts and expenditure in con- nection with the last horse parade in Warrington has just ,been issued. It states that the parade was cer- tainly the most. successful demonstration of its kind ever witnessed in Warrington, and fully justified the committee in the attempt they made in opening out and extending their efforts of the previous year. Perhaps the greatest difficulty the committee had to deal with was the nature Of the ground selected,which, being a public thoroughfare became inconveniently crowded and as a portion of the ground was occupied by Swing boats and stalls it very considerably hampered . the marshals in their duties, but it is expected that for the coming year a better provision will be made or what will be better still a more suitable site found. The statement of accounts shows that the receipts, in- cluding subscriptions amounting to £lOO 4s. (were Y-108 3s. Bd. After meeting all expenses there was a- balance in hand amounting to 3.:23 lOs 6d.---The next parade will be held on Saturday, May 2nd. There will be thirteen classes as follows :-1, brewers ; 2, railway and canal carriers ; 3, builders and builders merchants ; 4, contractors and carters; 5, tanners ; 6, Corporation ; 7, corn dealers and millers ; 8, Imineral water manufaeturers, grocers and bakers ; / 9, heavy miscellaneous ; .10, light miscallaneons ; 11, Ipair horse miscellaneous ; 12. fish dealers and milk dealers ; 13, coverad furniture vans.

As a SeClll6l to a collision which occurred in Liverpool- road, Warrington, on March 4th, Peter Domville, fanner New Barn Farm, Burtonwood, appeared before the War- rington magistrates onMonday, to answer to the charges of having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap in Liverpool-road, not having a lighted lamp attached to the vehicle, and furiously driving the horse. Mr. Crompton represented the defendant who pleaded not (runty. The facts of the case as alleged by the police were stated by Superinttndent 'Monaghan. He said that at a quarter to ten on Wednesday night, March 4th, an electric car was travelling from Sankey Bridges in the direction of the town, and when near the Coach and Horses, Herbert Smith, the driver saw the defendant and another man in a spring cart coming in the opposite direction. They were travelling at a, furious rate, and there was no light attached to the vehicle. The car driver used the emergency !make and brought the car to a standstill. He shouted, but the defendant took no notice and the cart crashed into the car. The stanchion of the.gate of the car was knocked off. The driver again called out to the defendant to stop, but he did not do so, and whipped his horse up, and galloped off. The driver reversed the car and fol- lowed the defendant to the terminus. He tried to rass him but could not as defendant was driving on the lines. When near the terminus the car driver left the car and caught hold of the horse's head. He called defendant's attention to the fact that he had no light, and asked for his name and address. Defendant was drunk and refused to give it, but the car driver saw that the name was painted on the vehicle. Herbert Smith, the driver of the car, gave evidence bearing out this statement, and also mentioned what transpired in an interview which he and Inspector Healey subsequently had with the defendant at Burtdn- Woor. Mr. Crompton contended that it was very improper to visit the defendant with Inspector Healey, who was not present at the time ef the accident, for the purpose of getting evidence against the defendant. Samuel Beaman, metal dealer, 221 Crosfield-street, cor- roborated as to the accident, but would not say that the defendant was drunk. _ _ .

Edgar Turner, tram conductor, and Inspector Healey were called, the last-named explaining that the reason why he went to Burtonwood to bake inquiries was because two Domville's resided there. • Robert Buckley Mellor, passenger on the car, Alfred B. Mellor, inspector at the Post Office, who saw the defendant Lathe tram terminus, and William Chadwick, who resides at Sankey Bridges, gave evidence. Chad- wick said the defendant was drunk, but the other wit- nesses whilst being of the opinion that defendant had had drink, could not say that he was drank. In his speech for the defence,Mr. Crompton protested against the visit to the defendant at'Burtonwood,which he contended was an improper way of getting up evi- dence. He thought they ought to be quite satisfied, after what three of the witnesses had said that the de- fendant was quite capable of managing the horse and trap. Three of the witnesses said they were not pre- pared to say that the defendant was drunk, and he thought that ought to settle the minds of the Bench on that point. With respect •to the charge of having no light, he would prove that the lamp was lighted by the ostler at the Woolpack before defendant started from Warrington.The defendant was well known in Warrington and had been attending the market for about 40 years. He had nothing whatever against his character. On the night in question the horse shied at the car and then bolted. _

Defendant gave evidence bearing out this statement. The ostler at the Woolpack stated that he lighted the defendant's lamp, which had a new candle in it, be- fore the vehicle left the yard. He would not say that defendant was sober but he was capable of driving a horse. The Chairman said the Bench' had thoroughly con- sidered the case, and there were two facts which stood out incontrovertibly. The defendant ran into the car, and instead of pulling up drove off furiously,but pulled up later, when he saw he was caught. With regard to Mr. Crompton's objection, he thought Inspector Healey was quite justified in ascertaining whether he was summoning the right man or not. The defendant would be fined ss. for drunkenness, ss. for not having a light. and 20s. for furious driving. He thought the Bench had dealt leniently with the defendant, seeing that the costs only amounted to .£3.

div.head: Warrington Drowning Mystery.
div.p: A Warrington Drowning Mystery.

On Sunday morning, William Warburton, a boat- man residing in Liverpool road, saw the body of a man floating in the Mersey 'near Litton's Mill. He gave information.to the police, and Constable Clarke recovered the.bod.r and conveyed it to the mortuary. The body was in an advanced state of decomposition and had evidently been in the water four or live weeks. Deceased was apparently be,twent 35 and_4o years of age, sft 4in. or Sin in height had brown hair, sandy moustache, and sandy side whiskers. The body was clothed in a blue serge coat and vest, brown tweed trousers, red, white and" blue striped cotton shirt,white flannel singlet, plaid silk neckerchief .tied in a sailor's knot„grey ribbed socks, and deceased had ofi' a pair of strong lace-up boots. The inquest was held at noon on Monday, before Mr. Brighouse coroner, when Detective Barlow', the .coroner's officer,said that there was no property on the body, which had not been identified. A verdict or " Found drothted " was returned.

div.p: Fire ;n Cattersby-lane.

Considerable damage was done by a fire which broke out in Battersbrlane on Monday afternoon. Information of the outbreak was received at the Fire ! -:lation at 3.20 and the fire bell having been rung ' Superintendent Turner and a number of men promptly turned out with the engine "Major." On reaching Battersby-lane it was found that three wooden build- ings' were ablaze, indeed the flames had obtained such a firm hold that the erections were completely des- troyed. The fire broke cut in the building occupied by the Empire Co operap.e Company, and c,-.icklv spread to the adjoining she'd and stable belonp• to Mr Razeldine, •plumber, and Mr. Bridge, Min dealer. Several horses were In the stable when the -atbreak was discovered but they were removed ,afely. A good supplrof water was obtained from a .! hydrants and it was not found necessary to use the engine. Despite the exertions of the brigade the buildings werej)nrnt to the ground, the tarred roofs falling an
- easy prey
to the flames. FOrtunately the firemen -ere successful in their efforts to prevent the fire from
. , spreading to an rdjoining orkshop. The loss sus- tained by Mr. Bridge is covered by insurance. It was 0.30 in the evening when the Brigade returned to the Fire Station.

div.head: GARDEN CITIES. Lecture at the Old Academy.
div.p: GARDEN CITIES. Lecture at the Old Academy.

Miss ILLINGWORTH, of Bradford, delivered an in- teresting and instructive lecture, illustrated by lantern views, on the Garden City movement, before the mem- berstof the Warrington Society on Thursday last week. His Worship the Mayor (Mr. J. C. Parr) presided and he was accompanied by the Mayoress. The CHAIRMAN, who had a cordial reception, made a few introductory observations. That was the first time, he said, he had had the pleasure of being under that roof which was hallowed with so many ancient memories and so many respected names. (Hear, hear). He felt that night that he was in the happy position of being a listener rather . than a speaker, and a learner more than a I teacher. The subject which was to be introduced I was one of vital importance to the community at large. I ' They were all interested in the welfare, and the educe- ; tion morally, and the improvement and development of ; our working classes. He took it that it was for the ' benefit of them especially that they were called together that evening. They all recognised the well-worn Latin motto "Mons sena, in corpore sano "—a healthy mind in a healthy body—(hear, hear)—and he thought that the ,corollary they might add with equal necessity was ! healthy habitations, and healthy and pleasant surround- , ings. (Hear, hear). It was with the view of promoting and encouraging this object that this very excellentand ' philanthropic institution had come into existence to make .its motives known and its benefits appreciated. The lecturer would no doubt illustrate and explain many points in the scheme which to the uninitiated might seem to bristle with difficulty. But with energy and I determination and care, many difficulties would be removed and he was sure he might promise to the lecturer their deepest anxiety and sincerest sympathy with the plans and proposals which she might have to suggest. (Applause). I Miss ILLINGIVORTH, who had a hearty reception, said the question of the housing of our people was a matter of vital importance to us as a nation. The wayl in which hundreds of thousands of our population were I condemned to live amid insanitary surroundings and in unhealthy dwellings was a matter which called for some prompt remedy. (Hear, hear.) They knew, of course, that a number of remedies had been suggested. Their corporate bodies possessed powers to deal with the question, but it was a reform which bristled with diffi- culties. The scheme she was going to put before them ' was known as the Garden City Scheme. It did not profess to be a perfectly easy and simple ' plan which 'could be put into operation to-morrow, but it was put forward as a practical scheme 1 and it was hoped that if the attention of the public I generally could be fixed upon it and it, Garden City broughtinto existence, it would be a valuable help in solving this over-crowded problem. (Hear, hear.) In ! dealing with the question they had to face the problems 1 of high rents and heavy rates in nearly all our modern cities, two factors which pressed the most heavily on the poorest portion of the population. The poorest 1 ' working classes paid more in rent in proportion to other people, than any other class of Society. In London this was particularly the case and was due to sweating landlords. She was not referring to landlords as a class but there were some landlords who made the ' would-be tenants of a workingclass home bid one against the other and the I rents were thus forced up to an abnormal figure. The I overcrowding was due to the influx of the people to the towns, and many of the people were compelled to live under conditions in which it was absolutely impossible for them to be physically healthy or morally strong. Reference was made to Mr.Rowntree's investigations at York, and a number of views were shown of life in the I slums of York,Birmingham and Bradford. The lecturer drew attention to the cellar dwellings of Bradford and pointed out that the prevalence of consumption was to some extent due to the dwellings in which we forced many poor people to dwell in.in giving a, sketch of Mr. Howard's scheme o f garden cities,the Lecturersaid in order to get our people back to the land again we should have to discover some attraction to take them back.At present there did not appear to be any. Some of the dwellings in the country, especially those of the labouring class, were as insanitary and uncomfortable as those in the slums. MT. Howard asked them to consider a plan whereby they could have all the advantages of the town and the country with none of these drawbacks. If only people were determined that there should be a garden city all the difficulties would promptly vanish. The ' main plank of the scheme was that the rents and 1 revenues which would be derived from the people who', lived in the garden city were to be vested in trustees for the benefit of the people. There was ' to be no private ownership in private land. ' The"unearned increment" was not to go into the pockets of private landlords but would be received by the trustees and spent upon the city. A plan of the suggested model city was shown on the screen. An estate of agricultural land having been bought, promoters would I proceed to carry out the scheme. Accommodation was ;provided for 31,000 inhabitants. The city would be ; circular and in the centre would be a large park;branching from this there would lie six main roads which would form the bounderies of the six wards into which the city would be divided. The streets would be wide and planted with, trees. The houses would have gardens round' each one of them and the 'style of architecture Iwould be varied according to individual tastes. On the outer ring of the city the manufactories ' would be erected but they would be driven by elec- tricity. Mill chimneys and the smoke nuisance would not be tolerated. A circular railway would encircle the city and around it would be farms and gardens. The lecturer expressed the belief that if cities could beferected on this plan it, would lead to a revival of agriculture as a good market would be placed within easy reach. The cities would not be allowed to grow 1 beyond the size stipulateci,but,it was proposed to link a : number of such cities together bv means of electric rail- ways. The scheme had been described as visionary and impracticable, but she contended that private enterprise had already shown that the scheme was practicable. The best instances in this country were those furnished by Messrs. Lever Bros. at Port Sunlight and by Messrs. Cadbury Bros. at Bourneville. Some beautiful slides were shown of the model dwellings at Port Sunlight and Bourneville and the lecturer asked her hearers to contrast the healthy appearance of the children with that of the children of the slums. In conclusion, the lecturer 'said the object of the Garden City Association was to arouse a deeper and wider in I terest in the question which had been discussed, and ; it their interest had been aroused she hoped they would form a branch in Warrington. The association had been formed to carry the scheme to a practical issue. 'The first issue of shares had been entirely taken up. We could not have too many remedies for the evil of over- icrowding. There were several remedies in the field already but She ventured to suggest that this one of a garden city was not only a desirable scheme but also a practical one. e Mr. LONG proposed a vote of thanks to the Lecturer, to the lanternist (Mr. Prith)and to the Mayor. He re- marked that however Utopian they might think the scheme was, lie was sure there were none who would not like to see it established in the neighbourhood of 1 Warrington.

Mr. Councillor BENNETT seconded the vote of thanks, and as an idealist, he expressed the opinion that what was best and most beautiful was ultimately the most practical. Mr. HALL supported the vote of thanks which was unanimously carried. Miss illingworth and the Mayor acknowledged the compliment and the meeting terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN POISONING CASE.
div.p: THE RUNCORN POISONING CASE.

On Friday at the Runcorn Police Court, Mr. R. Dobson, coroner, inquired into the circumstances attend- ing the death of Anna Mary Grubb, married woman, 18, White-street. Some time ago the deceased was brought , before the magistrates on a charge of attempted suicide. She had got into a depressed condition by drinking,and attempted to end her life by taking poison. She owed her recovery to the timely intervention of a police ser- geant, and two neighbours named Hannah Fryer and Sarah Davies. She was discharged on her friends pro- - mising to take care of her. Since than her health has gradually broken down, and she died on Thursday. Mr. F. Whalley was foreman of the coroner's jury, and Superintendent Ennion represented the police. The evidence showed that the deceased had spells of drink- ing. During one.on the 23rd August she swallowed the contents of a bottle of smelling salts contain- ing ammonia. The neighbours on either side of the house heard the fall of the woman and forced an entrance into the house. where Mrs. Grubb was found on the bedroom floor in an expiring condition. The women sent for Sergeent Bottom who ad-ninistered an emetic and her life was temporarily saved. The ammonia, Lhowever, set up ulceration of the throat which caused stricture,the taking of food being a matter of extreme difficulty. The deceased eventually died from exhaus- tion,and the jury returned a verdict that death was due to exhaustion caused by stricture of the gullet.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.
IRISH DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON. Visit ot Mr. John O'Donn3ll, M.P.

The Irishinea o Varrington celebrated the eve of St. Patrick's Day by a demonstration under the auspices of the local branch of the United Irish League of Great Britain. Mr. 'John O'Donnell, M.P. (for South Mayo) who was recently imprisoned in Ireland, and who gained some,notoriety for shaking his fist at Mr. Balfour in the House of Commons, and also for addressing the House in Gaelic was the central figure of the demon- stration. He was met at the railway station by Mt, James Roddy, the president of the local branch of the United Irish League and a number of members pro- minently connected with it. A torch-light procession was organised and Mr. O'Donnell and the local President drove through some of the principal streets of the town in a brougham. A brass band accompanied them and considerable enthusiasm was aroused. A meeting was held in the Co-Operative Hall, Winwick Street and a large number paid the stipulated sum of sixpence in order to gain admittance. The National Ethbletn was freely worn, both women ancL men sporting the "little bit of green." Mr. Roddy occupied the chair and there were also present Councillor Brophy, Messrs. F. L. Crilly (Liverpool), J. C. Dalton (Chester), D. Donnellan, M. Flanagan (Earlestown), McMahon. Hughes, Egan, J. Flanagan, M. O'Brien, T. Garman, M. Geraghty, and J. Haverley.

_ The CHAU:MAN said they were met once more for a I two-fold purpose. First to celebrate St. Patrick's Day —(applause)----and secondly to speak on the old, old story of the mis-government of Ireland from Dublin Castle. (Hear, hear.) They had an instance of this only last week in the county of Tipperary, where the police drew their batons and there was a perfect melee between the police and a number of tenant farmers who used their hire fists with effect. There was no reason for the inspector of police to order a baton charge,l but they hoped the day was not far distant ' in Ireland when the police would be utilised for doing that which was serviceable to the community at large (Hear hear.) ' The speaker proceeded to refer to the con- dition of Ireland to-day, and remarked that the best bone and sinew of the country was drifting to America. Under the present rule in Ireland, all the authority was behind landlordism with the bayonet and the baton in enforcing rack-rents. (Hear, hear.) Mr. DENNIS DONNELLAN moved the following resolu- tion :—" That we, the Irishmen of Warrington, express unabated confidence in the Irish Parliamentary Party and the United Irish League, and recognise and welcome the spirit which is widely evinced in this country in favour of setling the Irish land question upon the basis of making the Irish people owners of the soil which they till, and declare • the unalterable devotion of Irishmen to the principles- of national self govern- ment." (Applause.) They were present that night, he said, to hear an address from one of Ireland's represen- tatives—(applause)—one who had taken a very active part in the terrible struggle in the West of Ireland. Mr. O'Donnell was brought before a tribunal, presided over by two "removables." (Laughter.) A" removable "was an individual who was found nowhere else in the world but in Ireland, and he ivas supplied to Ireland by that civilizing government which was called the predomin- ant partner. (Laughter.) There was a prospert before i long of dispensing with the services of that ndividual. •and he (Mr. Donnellan). hopedhe would not have a rest- ing place anywhere else in the world. (Laughter.) It had been said they had come to that meeting to honour a criminal and to associate with criminals, (Laughter.) If Mr. O'Donnell was a criminal, then every Irishman was one. (Applause.) The - only college or -seminary that England ever provided for Ireland was a goal,which was the only place they could take their degrees from. (Laughter.) Ireland's census just issued was the saddest epistle ever read. Their population had decreased from eight to four millions, while the taxes had been in- creased. The production of Ireland was under forty millions; strictly speaking it was 31 millions. How was that mmiey spent? They.. were told that England was losing by Ireland and that Irishmen were a perfect nuisance. (Laughter.) The national exchequer in England took ten millions for doing nothing, the Irish landlord nine millions, and the County Council three millions. The worst feature, however, was the emigration. Forty thousand people left the shores of Ireland every year—(" Shame")—and it was estimated that everyone of them cost Ireland as a nation £2OO per head. The average age was 22. No nation could pros- per undersuch conditions, and no Irishmanwould rejoice more than they in England•would to have the question settled once for all. (Hear, hear.) " Mr. J. C. DALTON, Of Chester,-and formerly president of the Warrington branch, said it was necessary for the Irish people to get the ear of the honest British public. The British workingman had a conscience and it was for the Irish people to show him that what they were asking for Ireland was acceded in every part of the civilised globe. All the Irish wanted was self-govern- ment. (Hear, hear). There was no mystification abceit it. As Christians and God-fearing people they wanted justice and right and they intended to get it. A new era had dawned for Irelan4, and for England. The Irish had been subjected to a persecution which had no equal but they were willing to forgive that even at the eleventh hour. They would extend the hand of friend- ship, but they would have their full rights. Let Irish- Men do their duty to their country as Mr. O'Donnell had done—(applause)—and the day when Ireland would be great and glorious and free would not be delayed 24 hours. The English people were beginning to realise that Irish representatives were not mercenaries but that they were true patriots. If their hopes were soon real- ized there would be no need to die forlreland again,for they would be a great nation and Irishmen would have the right of making the laws for their own land. (Applause.) The resolution was carried with enthusiasm.

Mr. O'DoNNELL M.P., who on rising to speak, was cheered again and again, said it gave him the greatest possible pleasure to join with them in celebrating the coming of St. Patrick's day. They were met as ninny generations of Irishmen had met to celebrate one a the most important events in Irish history. (Applause.) Their presence that night wean proof that they were as readyas those who had gone before them to nicks every sacrifice to prove their fidelityto faith and fatherland. (Applause.) Through the instrumentality of the United Irish League they were determined to right Ireland's, wrong or know the reason why. Some -years ago they were divided but their organization was more powerful to-day than any organization which had existed in Ireland since the days of the Irish volunteers in 1798. Thej hadl,4oo branches, and they could put 1,400 battalions of staunch men in the field against Dublin Castle rule and Irish landlordism (Applause)., It had been agreed that landlordism must be a thing of the past. (Cheers). If the hopes held out to them during the past few mo'nths were not realized' there would be lively times for those who tried coercion and propped up landlordism in Ireland. If coercion had been smashed and landlordism abolished it was because of the determination of the Irish people. (Applause). Every man of the Irish race would have to be imprisoned be- fore they quenched the spirit of freedom (Hear, hear) It was hoped that the English newspapers and the English people would look upon them in a different light. He thought if they could only come to closer quarters the English would find they were not such bad fellows after all. Laughter). The English Government ought to be as ready to stand behind the Irish people as the Irish solliers were to stand behind the English battalions in South Africa (Loud Applause). Already there was a prospect of a better state af offairs. If the Government brought in a satisfactory Land Bill, that would end the agitation so far as the land question was concerned, but it would not prevent them asking for Home Rule. (Hear, hear,) They 'would not be content until Ireland managed her own affairs from College Green. They were only demanding that of which they were robbed a century ago, and what had been given to Canada, Australia, Cape Colony, and to the Boors. They were now pre- pared, after fighting for twenty years, to purchase peace. because if they got the Irish land question settled and the landlords removed from Dublin Castle and English influence, it would be thEO means of removing the last obstacle that stood in the way of Home Rule for Ireland. (Cheers.) The speaker proceeded to pass strictures upon Dublin Castle rule. He maintained that it was unnecessary to keep a police force of nearly 14,000 in a country where crime was almost unknown. in 'lreland the law was made for the classes and not for the masses, but the day was coining when the laws would be made for the masses and not for the classes. (Applause). The men of 1848 and H 97 were the men ; who paved the way for Irish freedom in the real sense of the word. (Hear, hear). They had calleathe atten- tion of the wcrld to the wrongs under which Ireland suffered, and to-day their successors had compelled the strongest of English Governments to legislate for them. The Irish had been a resolute and a fighting ,people. Their countrymen had shown their desire to act together, to fight together and oft-times they had died. together in furtherance of the Irish cause. Let them hope that the occasion would never arise again when they would have to die for the sake of , freedom. They hoped to win the cause they had at heart by constitutional means. He vtould ask them to close up their ranks. They were now merely waiting in anxiety to know what the result of the coming Land ' Bill would be. They were like an army waiting for the , bugle note to sound. They were waiting to see whether they would have to fight once more against landlordism with greater vigonrand determination. If they had not 1 to fight against landlordism they would have to renew the fight against Dublin castle rule and fight for "the old house on College ' Green." (Applause.) The speaker proceeded to show how the Irish party had co-operated with the workers of England in obt a i ing better conditions, and stated that there were many laws on the statute book which would nok have been passed foe the benefit of the workingmen of England if it had not been for the action of the Irish party. They i believed the working-classes were tI.S wrongly perAecuted as the farmers and labourers in Ireland. He thanked them for the work they had done in Warrington and ex- pressed the hope that they would strengthen their ranks, for by doing so they would be doing great, work for Ireland and helping forword the time when Ireland would be a nation. (Applause). Mr. F. L. t; (!ial'itl

League for Lancashire and Cheshire, addressed the meeting,and said there had not been the same activity in Warrington daring the last six or eight months that there was some time previously, but he hoped the present condition of affairs would lead to a revival of the Irish national spirit. Land reform, he said was no settlement of the Irish question. When that had been settled, it would pave the way for Home Rule. Mr. FLANA.GRAN, of Earlestown, proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. O'Donnell, and said Mr. O'Donnell was no traitor, but an honest patriot and a censistent repre- sentative of his constituency. (Applause.y Mr. Cannel'tor lI3OPHY seconded the vote of thanks, and said if the IVarrington branch swelled its nuaibers, Mr.O'Donnell would not, think he hadcome to Warring- ton for nothing. (Hear, hoar.) The proposition was unanimously carried. In acknowledging the compliment, Mr. O'DONNELL said if loving Ireland and hating Ireland's enextie3 con- stituted a criminal, than he was a criminal of the deepest dye. (Laughter and applause). The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman. '

div.head: BALL IN THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL..
div.p: BALL IN THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL..

A large number wore the nutional emblem in Warring- ton on St. Patrick's Day. Services were held in the Roman Catholic Churches, and were largely attended. The annuAl ball under the auspices of the Cnite,d Irish' League was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, -in honour of the Nationl.l festival. Dancing commenced at 8 p.m. to the strains of Mr. Burton's band. About 300 were present.

div.head: Celebration at Earlestown. The United Irish League.
div.p: Celebration at Earlestown. The United Irish League.

The seventh annual concert in connection with the Earlestown branch of the United Trish League was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday evening. A capital musical programme was gone through. such capable artistes as Miss Ignatius Beatty (soprano), Miss Alice Dannett (contralto), Mr. William Male (bari- tone), and Mr. Cannes Neary (humorist) having been engaged, whilst the Earlestown Orchestral Society's Band rendered selections at intervals. The chair was occupied by Dr. P. J. O'Keefe of St. Helens, the chief speaker being Mr. J. Cullinan M.P., for South Tipperary. The Chairman said that the manner in which they conducted their branch was such as to earn the respect and admiration of every honest Englishman. He had had every opportunity of observing and forming an opinion about the Davitt branch of the United Irish Lague at Earlestown and it had been a great source of pride for him to have seen the splendid efforts which formed that branch and the magnificent manner inwhich it was conducted.

Mr. Flannigan proposed the following resolution : "That this 'meeting of Irish Nationalists of Earlestown and District expresses its confidence in the Irish Parliamentary party under the leadership of Mr. John Redmond. That we pledge our unanimousallegiance to the policy of the United Irish League, to the efforts of which is due the present favourable outlook of the land question in Ireland. That we also cordially approve ef tae terms of the Land Conference as affording a basis of settlement of the Agrarian difficulty in Ireland." In proposing the resolution Mr. ,Flannigan said that they were asked to forget the past but ho would like to know from these people how could they as Irishmen, forget the past whilst they had the present in a worse form? He appealed to them, those of them who were sent from the homes of their childhood by those "alien adventurers "that pretended to govern Ireland, could they forget the past? The land bill now before Parliament ought to be extended to Irelandand he honed it would be. The moment the last link of the chain which bound Ireland had been broken, that was the moment for friendship between the Irish -and English people. He saw in the local paper the other week that the authorities bf this town were sending letters thanking a man who had been robbing and plundering them right and left, for presenting the people with a portion of their own God-given land. He was never more dis- gusted in his life. - Mr. Coswald seconded the res olution,an during a few remarks made in a similar strain as the first speaker he was continually interrupted by a member of the audi- ence who persisted in urging them to tight for their independence and do less talking, and asking did they want a better man than Davitt ? Silence was not obtained until the offender was forcibly ejected from the room. The same speaker referred to a suggestion made by Mr. Chamberlain to the •effect that the best way of settling the question was by reducing the Irish representation at Westminster. At the mention of the Colonial Secretary's name, derisive yells filled the hall and hooting and hissing was continued for some time. Mr. Cullinan M. P.,in supporting the resolution said that he wasextrernely sorry Mr.Farrell(the member for North Longford) has been unable to attend, as having come straight out of Sligo gaol he would have had a good many tit-bits to hurl at the English Government. Owing to the increased facilities for travelling, and the great development of new countries, the Irish people were leaving their own native soil to 'go and try to find a livelihood in lands of prosperito and wealth. They always found that an Irishman could reach the zenith of power in any land but his own. They found them in England, in highest office, in America, and on the Continent, they were at the top of the ladder, yet they never found one in distinction in his own country. Referring to the recent disturbance in the House of Commons the speaker said that when Mr. Wyndhau threatened them that if agitation continued in Ireland, they would be put last in any legislation, he (the speaker) got up and told him that they were not going to be humbugged like that. They never got anything out of England without they wrung it out of them. What was the reason that they were in the position in which they to-day found them- selves.? Was it because they sat quietly in the House of Commons like a lot of the English "fogies ?" Was it because they went to see the King crowned' and worshipped by a lot of idolaters. No! it was because they were not a subservient body, but adopted a fighting attitude that always oharacterised Irishmen. It had been said that they sided with the Boer; in the recent South, African War. They sided with the Boers, because they sympathised with any race fighting far their liberty and. independence. The English Government knew that they could make it as 'troublesome for them now as they did then. Tory members of the House had come to him (the speaker) and said "You Irishmen are fools; if you would only support the Government you would get anything you wanted for Ireland." If they had supported them, they would have scorned them and trampled them under foot. With reference to the land question, the- landlords had said that they were the real friends of England. In his opinion their loyalty was just about as deep as it concerned s. d. (A Voice: "That's true.") The usual votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

div.head: St. Mary's R.e. School, Earlestown.
div.p: St. Mary's R.e. School, Earlestown.

In celebration of St. Patrick's day, an entertainment was given in the above school on Tuesday evening, the first part of the programme being taken by the school children, and the second part, by elder members of the congregation. The children had been efficiently trained by Miss Browne (head mistress), Miss Darbyshire and the assistant teachers and considering that only a couple of weeks were spent in preparation, it was wonderful how well the children performed their tasks. The items submitted were :—Chorus ." Dear little Shamrock," "Little .Flo's brother" Miss ' Annie Bonney ; solo and chorus "Dear old home again," Miss M. Rush and the children ; dance "Fan dance"; song "Rock-a-bye" ; chorus "Erin the tear and the smile" ; dance "Merry revels " : chorus " The harp that once"; dance " Irish jig " "Miss C. Doyle and Master W. Merrick. This concluded the children's items and the remainder of the programme was supported by the Misses Battersby and Beatty, Messrs. O'Farrell, BAttersby, Highain and Unsworth. .

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOC IET Y.—The last meeting of the session in connection with the above, was held on Wednesday evening, in the Wesloyan.Sjhools. Mr. T. Gaudy occupied the chair, and after the minutes of the previous meeting had been read, called upon Mr. J. G. NVithinshaw to give his paper entitled " A trip across the Continent." The evening was a very enjoyable one, the lecturer giving a most interesting account of his visits through Germany and Denmark. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Withinshaw at the con- clusion, for his kindness in attending. Afterwards a short business meeting was held to appoint the new o'licers for next year, the following being unanimously elected :—Mrs. T. Gandy, president ; Mr. Parker, vice- president; Mr. E. W. Clarke, secretary ; Mr. J. 'l'. Ambler, treasurer. Mr. Parker. proposed a vote of thinks which was seconded by Mr. W. Moores, to the retiring officers and remarked on the succeasful season the Society had enjoyed. This was all the business.
