div.head: GREAT POiSONING CASE. TRIAL OF CHAPIIAN.
div.p: THE GREAT POiSONING CASE. TRIAL OF CHAPIIAN.
IQUETTE.

div.head: THREE CHARGES OF MURDER.
div.p: THREE CHARGES OF MURDER.

At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Monday before Mr. Justice Grantham, the trial was begun of George Chapman, otherwise.Seyerino Klosowski, 36, a publican, who is charged with the murder of Mary Isabella Snink, otherwise Mary Isabella Chapman; Elizabeth Taylor, otherwise Bessie Chapman; and Maud Marsh, otherwise Maud Chapman. The court was crowded. The Treasury Win represented b 7 the Solicitor General (Sir Edward Carson, K.C.), Mr. Sutton, Mr. C. Mathews, and ;qr. Bodkin. The prisoner was defended by Mr, GeOrge Elliott, Mr: A. Hutton, and Mr. V. Lyons. The. prisoner pleaded not guilty- to the indictments.

• Sir E. Carson opened the case for the Crown at some length. He dealt first with thecharge relating to Maud Marsh, who died on October 22, 1902, when the prisoner and Marsh were living together at the Crown public- house, High-street, Borough. The prisoner was the owner of that house,and was known and had been known for some time previously as George Chapman. This woman died under circumstances and with symptoms which baffled the skill of the doctor who attended her, and he very properly refused to give a certificate until a post-mortem examination had been held. The result of that examination was to prove that all the organs of the deceased woman's body were saturated with antimony while from the quantity found in the stomach there could be no doubt that shortly before her death a very lute dose of antimony had been administered. That she died of autimonial poisoning there could be no doubt. The question the jury had to decide was whether that antimony was administered by the prisoner or not. The Solicitor-General, proceeding, said it would be preyed beyond question that the prisener was a Russian Pole, and that in his youth he had been a sur- geon's assistant in a Polish hospital. They therefore started in the case with a man who in his early days had had considerable)trainine, in medicine and surgery. He came to England in l'BBB and wotked as a barber in several places in London, and for some time was known by his true name of Klosowski. In 1395, however, he appeared to have become acquainted with a girl named Annie Chapman, who lived. at Leytonstone, and the prisoner, it would seem, then adopted the name of Chapman, and from 1895 to 1902 he consistently bore that name. It would be proved that on April 3, 1897, the prisoner, who was at Hastings, where he kept a barber's shop, purchased from a chemist named Davidson an ounce of tartar emetic, which con- tained 437 grains. Two grains had been known to be a fatal dose, but ten to twelve grains would invariably be fatal. Counsel dealt briefly with the deaths of Isabella Spink and Bessie Taylor, in 1897 and 1901, respectively. With regard to Maud Marsh, he stated that she went to the Monument as the prisoner's barmaid, and related the Circumstances of the mock marriage between the girl and Chapman on October 12, 1001. In June, 1902, Chapman made the acquaintance of a girl named Rayner and asked her to go to America with him. She refused, saying, "Yon have got a wife down- stairs," to which he replied," Oh, I could give her that ad she would be no more Mrs. Chapman." It was this date which synchronised with the commencement of the illness of Maud Marsh and which ultimately terminatod in her death in October last.. During the course of her illness, Maud Marsh was taken into a. hospital and speedily recovered, but her illness returned after she went back to the prisoner, who, once referring to her illness, said, he could give her a bit like this and fifty doctors would not find it ont.": The prisoner alsotold nor sister that she was dying fast. If they were to make any distinction in the degrees of murder he sub- mitted that no typo of Murder was so malicious as that of poisoning, such as in the case before them, no murder more demonstrative of the cruelty of the culprit who could stand by the bedside of his victims day by thy, noting their sufferings and watching them sinking away. Mr. Elliott submitted that evidence could not be given of the death-of the two women Spink and Taylor, btit the Judge overruled the objection. Evidence as to the prisoner's history was given, and the case was adjourned.

The trial was resumed on Tuesday at the Old Bailey Mr. Elliott applied that the balance of a sum of money in the possession of the prisoner when arrested-should be handed over for the purposes of the defence. Counsel said the gold, .£155. had been .handed over, but there was a balance of £lOO in note § which the defence desired to have. The only ground for withholding the notes was that one of them might have been a portion of the money which belonged to Mrs. Spink. The Judge said he could not refuse the application under the idea that the notes might have formed part of the money of one of the deceased women: The money no doubt would be properly expended. He accordingly made the order asked for. ,Among the witnesses .called were Maud Marsh's parents, who reside at Croydon, and three of her sisters. it was stated that the deceased was 20 years of age. The cross-examination of her father was directed to show that Chapmananswered him in a perfectly frank mannev, and that his actions were open to everyone's observation, there being no attempt at concealment. The woman's married sister, Mrs. Morris, said she re- Marked to Chapman, "It is funny the doctors can't find out what is the matter with her" (Maud). "Oh," said the prisoner, snapping his fingers, "I could give her a . bit like that and
FIFTY DOCTORS WOULD NOT ,FIND IT OUT,

In cross examination this witness said her sister seemed to be fairly contented and happy with the prisoner, but used to complain that he would not allow her to go out. Witness tasted some of the champlgne ihtt NV,Li offered to Maud on one oceasion,but did not like it.
Mr. Elliott : Do you like champagne? The witness : Oh, yes, T like champagne, but I did not like that. It was different from any that I had ever drunk befare.
Another sister stated in cross-examination that Maud had_no_objectiOn to going to a hospital. _ _

• His Loidship therennon remarked that he was sur- prised hospitals should ask for charity and then look after the wives of licensed victuallers, who were hardly objects of charity. Mr. Elliot said that licensed victuallers would soon want all the charity they could get. His Lordship : hut not just yet.

. . Mrs. Jessie ':roon, the wife of a labourer, a customer at the Crown, told how prisoner engaged her as a nurse. She testified that everything she]gave to deceased was given to witness by prisoner. Maud was very thirsty. and witness used to fetch her water srom the tap until Mr. Chapman told her that whatever water was wanted she NVIS to fetch from the bar, and he would 'give it her.

CHAPMAN PREPARED THE FOOD. He prepared the milk, beef tea, and egg, &c., and ad- , ministered it himself. He would bring it into the room and would remove the tumbler which had contained it into the kitchen and wash it himself. Deceased was always in great pain after this nourishment had been so i administered. At times her limbs were stiff, . a.x 'though she were in a fit. One morning Mend's hands and a part of her arms were port wine coloAr, and her lips were black. Prisoner gave her brandy and water, but ! she would not drink Much of it, and asked for water. i Witness thdught it was perhaps too strong and so tasted it herself. It burnt her throat, and she washed her mouth. out. Cross-examined: She did not tell the doctor that deceased refused to take the brandy because it burnt her month. "Why not?" asked counsel. • "Because she was dead when the doctor arrived," replied witness. . The hearing was again adjourned.

' On Wednesday, Dr. Stoker, who attended Hand Marsh in her last illness, repeated the evidence he gave at the pelice court and inquest. He stated that he did not keep antimony, and had had none in his surgery for ten years. He did not put tartar emetic in his medicines. Cross-examined by Mr. Elliott, the witness said he had been ten yearS in practice, and had had considerable ex- perience in poisoning cases, but they had been canes of ptomaine poisoning. Mr. Elliott: You were not obstructed in any way by the prisoner in your attendance on the deceased or in your investigations ?e-Not in the slightest. The Judge: Were the symptoms in this °ease similar to those in the case of Beasie Taylor ?—Somewhat simi la r symptoms. I shoald have thought that would have ,made you • suspieions?—li did not until after death, when I began to think over the matter. But unfortunately not before death ?—No, not before . death. I Dr. Stephenson, one of the official analysts to the Home &lice, said he .made an autopsy on the body of Maud Marsh. He found no evidence of any natural disease that would account for her death. He analysed ; the various organs, and in all of them he found anti- mony. There were traces of arsenic, but the quantity ; was very small. After this analysis he came to the con- elusion that death was due to poisoning by antimony administered in a soluble form, and that a large dose of ! antimony had been adminstered just before death. The quantity of antimony found indicated that some 25 to 30 grains of tartar emetic had been given. Antimony had no pronounced taste, and the taste could easily be concealed in food or drink, The Solicitor General: Having made this Analysis you say there is nothing to account for death except poisoning by antimony? The witness : Nothing. .In cross-examination Dr. Stephenson said the inunedi- ete cause of death was gastro-enteritis. Ptomaine poisoning could set up this complaint, but he had never I come across a case of the kind in which the enteritis was so extensive. Tartar emetic was given to persons I who were addicted to drinking to ;cure them of the habit. It caused nausea, and thus set persons against I. the drink with which it was mixed. There was not sufficient arsenic to indicate that death might have been •I caused by arsenical poisoning apart from antimony. I In re-examination the witness said he found nothing to suggest that the woman had been addicted to drink, •
and it had never been suggested to him until just now in cross-examination that she had been of drunken habits.
Sir Edward Carson asked Dr. Stephenson whether ptomaine poisoning by any conceivable process could produce antimony in the blood ?—" Oh, no," answered the witness.
The prosecution next called evidence in the case res.! pecting Isabella Spink. In answer to the Judge, Sir E. Carson said the certi- ficate of death attributed it_to phthisis.

div.head: Isaballa Spink's Death.
div.p: Isaballa Spink's Death.

This concluded the evidence with regard to Maud Marsh, and in .reply to the Judge as to which case they w ere going into next, the Solicitor-General said he would go Into the case of Isabella Spink. The medical evidence wa.s the most interesting in this case. The woman died on Christmas Day, 1891; and phthisis was given as the cause of death in the certificate. . Dr i Stevenson again went into the box, and said the condition of the body was "quite remarkable." The body might have been coffine4 that day instead of five years previously. An .analysis of the organs showed that they contained 383 grains of emetic tartar, and he came to the conclusion that death was due to poisoning by antimony. In cross-examination, Dr. Stevenson said that bodies placed in lead coffins often kept in a state of remark- able preservation for years—as in the case of Charles I.

div.head: Bessie Taylor of Lymm. How She Met With Her Death.
div.p: Bessie Taylor of Lymm. How She Met With Her Death.

This concluded the evidence, and the case of Bessie Taylor, of Lynun, was proceeded with. William Taylor, a brother of the deceased, said in December, 1900, witness went to see his sister when she was at the Monument, and found her very ill. Subse- quently he was informed of her death on February 13, 1901, and he was present at the funeral in Lymre, Cheshire.

Murtha Stevens, of Barkin6,who nursed Bessie Taylor at the Monument,deposed that Bessie was often severely sick, and complained of a burning sensation . in her throat. Frequent thirst was another symptom. Dr. Stoker spoke to attendingrißessie Taylor. The symptoms were similar to those noted in, the other eases.

On restting on Thursday, Mr. Justice Grantham was handed a letter by one of the jurors, who was employed at the St. George's Hospital, and he read as follows : Dear Sir,—l do not think we shall want your services after this week. Sorry you are detainedat the Law Courts.—Yours faithfully,— The letter w.ts signed by the secretary of the hospital, and the Judge added: Well, if the meaning of this is that because you are detained here doing your duty as a. citizen you are therefore•dismissed, all I can say is that it is a most discreditable thing. I will not say more now because there may be some explanation, but it is very unfortunate, to say the least, that this should have happened in this case and at this time. I will write myself to the secretary of the hospital, and ask someone to come here from the hospital. There may be some explanation.
RFISSIE TAYLOR'S REM AI"JrS.

Dr. Stephenson was then called, and proceeded to give the analysis of the contents ot the stomach of Bessie Taylor, who died on February 13, 1901. The body was in a good state of preservation. The inner surface, of the bowels was coated throughout their whole length with an orange yellow substance, sulphide of antimony. He found no trace of natural disease which could account for death. The cause of death was gastro enteritis, arising from an irritant poison, and the only irritant poison which he coldd find in the body was antimony.
A BEG DOSE OF POISON.
A large quantity of antimony in the bowels indicated that a big dose of the poison had been taken just prior to -death.

Cross-examined: The body had been buried about 20 months, and when it was exhumed it was found to be covered with fungi or "vegetable mould." The fade was not so perfectly preserved as was that of Isabella. Spink. The latter's was a unique case. Witness ex- plained that the time of burial and the dryness or dampness of the ground would be factors to be taken into,consideration. Antimony would not prevent the growth of mould, and this wOuld alter the featuies.
EVIDENCE OF ARREST.

Detective-Tnspector Godley gave evidence of the prisoner's arrest on Saturday, October 25. "Maud Marsh, who has been living with you as your wife," said witness to the prisoner, "has been poisoned by arsenic, and from the circumstances I shall take you to the police station while I mike inquiries." " I know nothing about it," was the prisoner's comment. "I don't know how she got the poison. She has been in Guy's Hospi- tal for the same sort of sickness." Prisoner was then conveyed to the police station and witness searched the house, finding the medicine' bottles, powders, and other things produced. A revolver fully loaded was also dis- covered. Notes and gold to the value of £268 were found. Among the papers found at the house was a letter indicating that prisoner had been in communica- tion with a firm of property agents for the disposal of the Crown public-house. The same evening witness charged him with the murder of Maud Marsh. "I am innocent," was his reply. On December 21 witness charged prisoner with the murder of Isabella Spinkand 13ess1e Taylor, chargin,, him in the-. name of George Chapman, otherwise Severing Klosowski. "I don't know the other fellow," prisoner 'commented. "That's you," said the witness.
Inspector Kemp gave corroborative evidence. NO EVIDENCE FOR THE DEFENCE.

Mr. Elliott said he would call no witnesses for the defence, and proceeded to address the jury. He fully admitted the magnitude of the task before, him, especi- ally as the Solicitor-General by virtue of his position as an officer of the Crown had the right to reply. The case unfortunately had been urrounded by ri storm of prejudice which in every other country might imperil the calm administration of justice.

div.head: TEE ALIEN BIAS.
div.p: TEE ALIEN BIAS.

He warned the jury against one "insuperable diffi- culty" with which they were confronted in exercising their duty—the fact that the prisoner was a stranger in this country—an alien, and he pleaded with them to overcome any natural bias that they Might have in that matter. • It was impossible to disguise the fact that throughout the land there was a sense of distrust and suspicion with regard to the number of aliens poured upon those shores.

div.head: ABSENCE OF MOTIVE.
div.p: ABSENCE OF MOTIVE.

If the jnry had before them a man bound by the ties of matrimony to a woman from whom his love and affec- tion had passed and who had 'conceived for another• woman an overmastering passion, and he saw that the only course for the gratification of his wish lay through .the tomb of his wife there would be a motive. But in this case there was not the slightest necessity for Chap- man to resort to any violent measures to rid himself of the woman of whom he had tired. They looked in vain, said counsel, for any motive in this *case. Unless they were satisfied beyond doubt that this hideous charge had been substantiated then whatever might be their . private feelings they must give the prisoner the benefit of the doubt. Dealing with the questionof the posses- sion of poison by the prisoner he pointed out that with the exception of the statement of Mr. Davidson, the Hastings chemist,- who stated that he sold prisoner poison in 1817 there was not the slightest evidence that prisoner had any poison in his possession until they came down to the time of his arrest, when a small quantity of antimony was found in the rinsings .of bottle which had contained -bismuth. Whether or not the prisoner Chapman was the Russian Klosowski was a matter for the jury to determine, and if he were there was this point in his favour, that the women who had come- forward to recognise him and who had the same relations with him as the dead women themselves, had not suffered from his malpractices. If he had made no' attempts on the life of those women why should he have sought to take the lives of the three women mentioned in the charge? • THE J [THY MIN'S NOTICE. .

After the adjourn.ment for luncheon, the secretary of St. George's Hospital attended and explained that the letter to the juryman was simply an at of kindness. He had been employed as an extra clefc fora few weeks and was really not entitled to any notice. - The juryman S4id he thought he was entitled to a week's notice, but the Judge said he had nothing to do with that, and the se !rotary havirig promised an extra week's salary the incident closed.

div.head: .PRISONER STILL TAI.:ING NOTES.
div.p: THE .PRISONER STILL TAI.:ING NOTES.

The prisoner's attitude during his counsel's .speech was the same as it had been throughout the greater part of the trial—he sat forward on his chair in the dock,his knees cre.ssed, basily taking notes. His attention Wits bent 9n this work, and he sat there heedless, apparently of the words uttered on his behalf. Mr. Elliott laid emphasis on the circumstances brought out in the evidence that Chapman was always ready to obtain for Bessie Taylor everything—wines and other things—that Were recommended by the doctors. He had courted investigation by the readiness with which he had con sented to other medical Teen of more or less eminence being summoned to the case, he had made no objection to the mother's attendance upon her daughter, and he had readily engaged nurses. Could any man have done more for the welfare of a sick wife? No fewer than three doctors, besides Dr. Stoker, were called in with the acquiescence of the prisoner, who readily paid their fees, and each doctor diagnosed the complaint differently. It was not sur- prising; ad led counsel, after the conflicting medicines and different treatment of the various doctors that Bessie Taylor died. In the case of Maud Marsh it ha d been suggested that the prisoner deliberately murdered her to marry Florence Raynor, but why should he have done that when all he need have done•was to tell Maud Marsh to go, as he had no claim upon him. Or he might' have gone away himself. He was willing to go to America at that time. The illness of Maud Marsh had indeed nothing to do with the appearance on the scene of Florence Raynor. Counsel said it.was trite that antimony had been found in the bodies of the three women, but there was no evidence to show that at the time when prisoner was living With the three women he had any tartar emetic in his possession.

div.head: CILAPNI AN SOBBING FREELY.
div.p: CILAPNI AN SOBBING FREELY.

Tn concluding a speech of two hours duration, Air. Elliott made a powerful appeal to the feelings of the jury. Meanwhile Chapman, with his hankerchief to his eyes, was sobbing freely. Mr. Elliott in concluding his speech for the defence, was slightly applauded by those in Court as he resumed his seat.

In his reply, the Solkitor-General asked—Was not motive shown in the history of the prisoner's unbridled. heortless, cruel lust? In this case, all the facts, the identity of the symptoms, the identity of the suffering of these poor women, and the results of the post-mortem and the scientific analysis—all these pointed to the prisoner's guilt.

THE .JUDGE AND THE DOCTORS. Mr. Justice Grantham, in summing up, said it was a • sad reflection that a man should have been able to carry' on these practices for a number of years, defying several medical men. Dr. Stoker saw Maud Marsh. dying by inches in the greatest agony from an irritant poison. Why did he not inquire? If it had not been for Mr. and Mrs. Marsh, who had no knowledge of Medicine, no discovery would probably have been made, And other victims would most likely have been added to the list. It was not till -Dr. Gra.pel appeared on the scene, at the request of Mr. and Mrs. Marsh, that any real medical intelligence was brought to bear on the case. He was forry to have had to make this comment, but doctors should be alive to the matters. There was a series of misadventures with regard to the way in which the doctors exercised what- they called their skill: Shame to say, it did not end with these practitioners. Something of the same kind was found in connection with one of the finest institu— tions in the world—Guy's Hospital. Ho did not say that they ought to have found it out, but it was abomin- able that a woman should go into the hospital, and that they were there unable to discoveranything. AGAINST CREMATION. 110. hoped the case would be a warning to people who- wished to shut up their church-yards and have every- body burned, because if that came to pass they might depend upon it that it would lead to a considerable pa- crease in the number of poisoning- cases. •It was a pleasure to know that with our scientific knowledge we were able, after such a lapse of years, to clear up a mystery of this character. They could not fora minute hesitate to believe the evidenze of D. Stevenson. His evidence was unimpeachable. n each of these three cases there was only one person who had unrestricted access to the women, and who was shown to b& in possession of ontimo.ny, and he was the prisoner. . . THE .JURY'S VERDICT. During the closing sentences of the judge's summing. up, the prisoner broke down again and wept. Having concluded his address his lordship left the bench, 'and prisoner was conducted below. The court at this time was packed to . suffocation, some ladies even being seated on the bench.

The jury returned into 'Court in twelve minutes, and. prisoher was again conducted, weeping into the dock. He had to be assisted to the rail, and a warder stood on each side. The foreman of the jury having returned a :441 verdict of guilty, the prisoner was asked if he had any- thing to say why sentence should not be passed upon him according to law. The prisoner, who was deathly pale, and had to be supported by the warders; made n,, answer.

LAST WORDS OF TUE JUDGE. The Judge, assuming the black cap,. then passed sentence of death in these terms :—.Severmo Klosowski —I decline to call you by the English name you have. chosen—the only satisfactory feature in the case is that I am able to address you as a foreigner, and not as an Englishman. The jury have come to the only conclu- sion that anyone who has heard this case could come to, and it is not necessary for me to go through the hartowing details, nor to refer again to the frightful cruelty of which you have been guilty in murdering year by year the women on whose bodies you had. gratified your vile •lust. I have but one duty to per- • form—it is not necessary to say more—it is the duty of passing sentence of death. Sentence of Death. His Lordship then delivered I sentence in the usual form. Prisoner,who by this time was almost in a state: of collapse, was then assisted to the cells by a couple of warders.

Theft From Earlestown Market. At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Georgina Wilkinson, the wife of a collier living on Newton Common, was charged with having on the 13th March, stolen four children's pinafores, and an apron, of the value of IS. 101 d., the property of James Barrow, a draper, residing at 44, Dallam-lane, War— rington. The evidence showed that the prosecutor has a stall in Earlestown market, and at 8 p.m. on the ,night in question P.C. Lenny was on duty in plain clothes when he saw the prisoner standing against the stall. She had a 'shawl over her head. She picked up the articles,put them under the shawl, walked away to a dark part of the market, and then put them in a bag she carried in her hand.--Inspector Foster said numerous complaints of petty larcenies in the marke t had been received and constables had been placed on duty in plain clothes to detect offenders. Prisoner's husband was in a delicate state of health, and as that was her first appearance he thought the justice of the case would be met if she were dealt under the First Offenders Act.—The magistrates consented and the prisoner was bound over to appear when c,lied upon/

Fire Brigade's Experiments at Winwick. Some interesting operations were conducted at W Jll wick Asylum on Saturday afternoon by Superintendent' Turner and nine other members of the Warring.tou Fire Brigade, the object being to see what provistou had been made in case of an outbreak of fire, to familiarize the brigade with the position of the hydrants, and to ascertain the capacities of the fire engine " Captain " for throwing water over the build- ings. The brigade were accompanied by Alderman Smethurst (chairman of the Fire Engine Committee), Councillor Peacock (deputy-chairman),and Councillors Barton, Brophy, Brough, Duncan, and William- Roberts. Unfortunately, a strong wind was blowing .at the time and prevented the water reaching to the top of some of the buildings, but it is believed that under ordinary circumstances all points would havi been easily reached. The experiments, were con- sidered to be very satisfactory. Good Templary. The usual weekly session of the Temperance gis- sion Lodge of the 1.0.G-.T. was held on Wednesday evening in Ebenezer Church. Bro. P. Bate presided over a good attendance. After the usual business, Bro. C. J. Sheath referred to the death of Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., and moved that a vote of condolence be entered on the minutes, stating that the cause of tem- perance could ill afford.to lose such men as him. Bro. O'Brien seconded, and the resolution was carried- The programme was "Irish Night," and the follow" ing programme was given :—Song, " Terence's fare- well," Bro. C. J. Sheath; readng, "Rory O'More's present to the priest," Bro. J. Wareham; song, ,c One of the rank and file." Bro. O'Brien ; song, "The meeting of the masters," Sister Mrs. Sheath. Addresses were given during the evening by Bros Smith and O'Brien.
